title: The life cycle of a flowering plant: how fruit ripens, how plants time their lives, and how they end
playtest: Read step by step as a parent and child in a city flat would use it. Everything in the spine, the ripening bag test, uses mangoes, a banana and paper bags. Not yet run at home: please check these. First, the gap between the three mangoes can be small, one or two days, so choose the hardest green mangoes and a very ripe banana, and say so if the mangoes look the same. Second, in the leaf test, the order of yellowing, with the banana box first, then the dark box, then the light, is expected but not certain. Third, money plant cuttings usually root in a week to ten days, and a cutting with a leaf is expected to root best, but the leafless ones may root just as well. Fourth, the marigold project needs eight weeks and a sunny balcony, and with only three plants in each group, the difference can be small. Fifth, the fern spore step needs a fern with ripe brown dots, and growing the spores is optional and may not work. Sixth, the tomato test depends on the room's warmth. The two games have their cards written out in full, and One Season or Many can be played alone. Feasibility review: mangoes are out of season for part of the year, so the ripening tests also work with green bananas from one hand. The tomato test now runs to day 12 because shop tomatoes can be slow. Still to check at home: the leaf-yellowing order, how long money plant and fern spore steps take in your weather, and the marigold difference with only three plants per group.

summary.text: A hard green mango sits in a paper bag with a very ripe banana. The two never touch, yet the mango turns soft and yellow days before a mango left alone. Something travels through the air between them. Your child tests the ripening gas, watches leaves give up their green, and roots cuttings from nodes. Then the unit looks at the whole shape of a plant's life: plants that flower for one season or many, plants that save food for a second year, ferns that grow from dust, and trees that keep a diary in their rings.
summary.art: Two paper bags on a kitchen counter. In one, a green mango leans on a spotted yellow banana. In the other, a green mango sits alone. A hand presses the first mango, which is soft.

intro.hook: Take two hard green mangoes. Put one in a paper bag with a very ripe banana. Put the other in a paper bag alone. Wait four days and press both. The mango that sat with the banana is usually softer. The banana never touched it. So how could one fruit change the other?
intro.text: Ripening looks like something each fruit does alone, slowly, as time goes by. But a ripe fruit also sends out a gas that changes the fruit next to them. In this unit you test that gas. You also find out why a leaf turns yellow, where a new money plant can grow roots, and how long different plants live. Some plants flower for a single season and some flower for hundreds of years. At the end you will see a plant's life as a whole, from the first leaf to the last.
intro.art: A kitchen shelf with a ripe banana beside a mango, and faint wavy lines in the air between them, drawn as if you could see the gas.

outcomes: I can explain that ripe fruit gives off a gas called ethylene, which helps nearby raw fruit to ripen, and use this to plan and test ripening at home.
I can say what changes inside a fruit as it ripens, and why a fruit gets soft, sweet, coloured and scented.
I can explain what a leaf is doing when it turns yellow, and what ethylene and darkness do to leaves.
I can sort plants into annual, biennial and perennial, and into plants that flower in one season and plants that flower in many.
I can explain how plants tell the season, using day length and cold, and why coriander and palak go to seed in summer.
I can describe the life cycle of a fern, from spore to tiny heart-shaped plant to a new fern, and say how it differs from a flowering plant.
I can explain why a plant grown from a cutting is a copy and a plant grown from a seed is a little different, and why that matters.
I can say what a tree ring records, and describe the different ways scientists think about how long a plant can live.

terms.meaning: The set of changes that turns a hard, sour, green fruit into a soft, sweet, coloured and scented one.
terms.example: A raw mango is hard and sour. A ripe mango is soft, sweet and yellow.
terms.art: A raw green mango beside a ripe yellow mango cut open.

terms.meaning: A simple gas made by plants, with two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms. Ripe fruit give off a lot of it, and it tells nearby fruit to ripen.
terms.example: A ripe banana in a bag gives off ethylene, and a raw mango in the same bag ripens faster.
terms.art: Wavy lines drifting from a ripe banana to a raw mango inside a paper bag.

terms.meaning: The planned ageing of a leaf, a fruit or a whole plant. The plant takes the leaf apart in an orderly way and moves useful materials to other parts.
terms.example: A yellowing leaf in autumn or dry season is in senescence.
terms.art: A leaf that is green at the stalk and yellow at the tip, with small arrows moving from the leaf into the stem.

terms.meaning: A plant that takes two years to finish their life cycle. In the first year they grow leaves and store food. In the second year they flower, make seeds and die.
terms.example: Carrot, beetroot and onion are biennials.
terms.art: A carrot plant in year one with leaves and a fat orange root, and in year two with a tall flower stalk.

terms.meaning: A plant that lives for many years and flowers in many seasons.
terms.example: Mango, neem and coconut trees are perennials.
terms.art: A mango tree with flowers and fruit, beside a calendar showing many years.

terms.meaning: The length of the day and night. Many plants use it to tell the season.
terms.example: In summer the days are long and the nights are short.
terms.art: A sun and a moon on a see-saw, with a long day on one side and a long night on the other.

terms.meaning: A spell of cold that some plants need before they will flower. Scientists call it vernalisation.
terms.example: Tulips and apples need a cold spell before they flower.
terms.art: A bulb in cold soil under snow, followed by the same bulb flowering in spring.

terms.meaning: A tiny single cell, much smaller than a seed, that can grow into a new plant. Ferns, mosses and mushrooms make spores.
terms.example: The brown dust under a fern leaf is full of spores.
terms.art: A fern leaf turned over to show rows of brown dots, with a magnified spore beside it.

terms.example: A fern frond is cut into many small leaflets.
terms.art: A curled young fern frond opening into a full frond.

terms.meaning: The tiny, flat, heart-shaped plant that grows from a fern spore. The tiny plant makes eggs and sperm.
terms.example: A prothallus is only a few millimetres wide and grows on damp soil.
terms.art: A tiny bright green heart-shaped plant on damp soil next to a coin for size.

terms.meaning: A root or stem that swells up to store food for later, so that a plant can restart after a dry or cold season.
terms.example: Carrot, potato, ginger and onion are storage parts.
terms.art: A carrot, a potato, a ginger root and an onion in a row, each labelled with the part of the plant it is.

terms.meaning: A thick stem that grows sideways under or along the ground. New shoots and roots come from it.
terms.art: A piece of ginger with a young green shoot and thin roots.

terms.meaning: A new shoot that grows from the base or roots of a plant. It becomes a new stem.
terms.example: A banana plant sends up suckers around their base.
terms.art: A banana plant with a smaller banana shoot growing from the base.

terms.meaning: Joining a twig from one plant onto the roots and trunk of another, so that the two grow as one plant.
terms.example: Most Alphonso mango trees are grafts, not grown from a stone.
terms.art: A mango twig tied with tape onto a young rooted mango stem.

terms.meaning: A plant that is an exact copy of another, made without seeds. Cuttings, suckers and grafts make clones.
terms.example: A money plant cutting is a clone of the vine it was cut from.
terms.art: A money plant vine with a cutting in a glass of water, joined by a dotted arrow.

terms.meaning: A ring of wood that a tree adds in a growing season. In places with a dry or cold season, one ring is usually one year.
terms.example: Count the rings on a cut branch to count the years.
terms.art: A cut log with dark and light rings and a ruler laid across it.

terms.meaning: A tree that drops all their leaves in the dry or cold season, then grows new ones.
terms.example: A teak tree is deciduous. A mango tree is evergreen.
terms.art: A teak tree with bare branches in the dry season and the same tree covered in big leaves in the rains.

terms.meaning: How long a living thing lives.
terms.example: A moong plant has a lifespan of about three months.
terms.art: A long horizontal bar with a moong plant at one end and a banyan tree at the other.

explanations.concept: What ripening is, and why fruit do it
explanations.definition: Ripening is a set of changes that turns a hard, sour, green fruit into a soft, sweet, scented, coloured one. It happens when the seeds inside are ready to travel.
explanations.description: A raw mango is hard, green and sour. This helps the fruit, because animals leave the fruit alone until the seeds are ready. When the seeds are ready, the fruit changes. Enzymes cut the starch stored in the fruit into sugar, so the fruit tastes sweet. Other enzymes loosen the walls between the cells, so the fruit gets soft. The green chlorophyll is taken apart, and yellow and orange substances that were hidden underneath show, or new red ones are made, as in a tomato. Acids fall, so the sour taste fades. Tiny scent molecules are made, and these are what you smell from across a room. Each change is a signal to a bird, a bat, a monkey or a person that the fruit is ready to eat. The animal carries the seeds away. Ripening is a fruit asking to be eaten.
examples: A green banana is starchy and hard. A yellow banana is sugary and soft.
A green tomato turns red as a red substance called lycopene is made.
A raw mango is sour. A ripe mango is sweet, and you can smell it from across the room.
explanations.art: A raw mango and a ripe mango, each cut open, with labels for hard, sour and green on one and soft, sweet and yellow on the other.

explanations.definition: Ethylene is a gas that plants make. It is a hormone that travels through the air, and it tells fruit to ripen. Ripe fruit make a lot of it.
explanations.description: Ethylene is one of the simplest chemicals a plant makes, with just two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms. A raw fruit makes a tiny amount. When the fruit begins to ripen, the fruit makes much more, and the gas drifts out into the air. A raw fruit nearby can sense the gas with receptors, which are proteins that catch it. In 1993, a team that included Caren Chang found the first of these receptors in a small plant. Sensing the gas makes the raw fruit make ethylene too, so the ripening spreads like a chain reaction. Fruit that ripen like this after they are picked, such as banana, mango, papaya, tomato, guava, apple and sapota, are called climacteric. Fruit such as grapes, oranges, pineapple, strawberries and watermelon do not ripen more after picking. Ethylene also yellows leaves and makes flowers and leaves drop. In sealed plant chambers, such as those used in space research, the gas has to be removed, or it builds up and harms the plants.
examples: A ripe banana in a closed bag speeds up a raw mango, a raw papaya or a hard green tomato in the same bag.
A bunch of spinach next to a ripe banana yellows sooner, because the gas also pushes leaves to age.
A grape picked green will stay sour. It will not ripen in a bag.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a paper bag with a ripe banana, a raw mango and a raw tomato, and wavy lines from the banana to the other fruit.

explanations.concept: Ripening at home, and what not to do
explanations.definition: You can ripen a hard fruit at home by keeping it warm and close to a ripe fruit in a loosely closed bag or box. Cold stops ripening, and a sealed space with no fresh air spoils the fruit.
explanations.description: Ripening works best at ordinary room warmth, about 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. In a refrigerator, ripening stops, and fruit from warm places such as mango, banana and tomato can be damaged by the cold, with dark skin and patchy colour. So ripen first, then cool a ripe fruit if you want to slow it. A paper bag or a loose cardboard box holds the gas close to the fruit, and a ripe banana or apple supplies it. Open the bag every day to let fresh air in, because fruit breathe, and in a sealed space the oxygen falls and the fruit turn sour and spoil. Families in many parts of India have long ripened mangoes in a heap of straw, rice or paddy husk, which holds the gas and the warmth, and they did not need the word ethylene. Some traders use a grey stone called calcium carbide to ripen fruit fast. Food safety rules in India do not allow this, because it can leave harmful dirt on the fruit. Ethylene gas itself, used in small controlled amounts, is allowed.
examples: A paper bag with a ripe banana and a green mango, opened each morning to let in air.
Mangoes in a box of rice or straw, as many families do in the mango season.
A green tomato on a kitchen shelf ripens in a few days, but in the fridge it stays green and pale.
explanations.art: A cardboard box with a loose lid on a warm shelf, holding mangoes and ripe bananas, and a hand lifting the lid to let in air.

explanations.concept: Do plants send messages through the air?
explanations.description: Ethylene is one gas that plants send into the air, and many plants release other scent molecules when a caterpillar chews them. In 1983, two American scientists, Ian Baldwin and Jack Schultz, reported that poplar and sugar maple saplings with chewed leaves seemed to warn untouched saplings nearby. The untouched saplings made more bitter chemicals in their leaves. Later experiments on wild sagebrush by Rick Karban and others also found that plants near a damaged plant suffered less damage. Plants can sense and answer these gases. Scientists still argue about what to call it, and some of the early experiments were hard to repeat. The question is whether a damaged plant is warning others, or whether the neighbours are only overhearing a smell.
examples: A raw fruit senses ethylene from a ripe fruit next to them and starts to ripen.
Cut grass gives out a fresh smell, which is a chemical alarm that other plants nearby can sense.
Sagebrush near a damaged sagebrush was chewed less by insects.
explanations.art: Two plants in a field. The left one is chewed by a caterpillar and gives off wavy lines. The right one catches the lines and its leaves turn darker.

perspectives.explanation: Plants release chemicals when they are damaged, and neighbours sense them and prepare. This is a form of communication, even though no plant has a brain. The messages are real, and they change what the receiving plant does.

The damaged plant releases chemicals as a by-product of the damage, and the neighbours happen to overhear. Calling it a warning puts a purpose where there may be none, and some experiments have been hard to repeat.

explanations.definition: Senescence is the planned ageing of a leaf. The plant takes the leaf apart in order and moves the useful materials to the stem, the roots or the seeds.
explanations.description: A leaf does not simply die. It is taken apart, like a shop being emptied before closing. First the green chlorophyll is broken down, and the nitrogen it contains is sent out through the leaf stalk. Yellow and orange substances were hidden in the leaf all along, and they show once the green goes. Proteins are cut up and moved, and sugars and minerals follow. At last the leaf stalk seals itself, and the empty leaf falls. In a crop such as wheat or rice, a large part of the nitrogen in the grains is moved there from older leaves, according to measurements. A leaf that is kept in the dark cannot make food, and it is taken apart much sooner than a leaf in the light. Ethylene speeds the process up. That is why a bunch of palak yellows faster in a closed dark cupboard next to ripe bananas.
examples: A moong plant's lower leaves turn yellow while the pods fill. Their materials are moving into the seeds.
A covered patch of a leaf goes yellow while the uncovered part stays green.
Coriander kept in the fridge next to ripe fruit goes yellow sooner.
explanations.art: A leaf yellow at the tip and green at the stalk, with small arrows showing sugars and minerals moving down the stalk into the stem.

explanations.concept: Why does an annual plant die after making seeds?
explanations.description: Moong, rice, wheat and sunflower plants die soon after their seeds ripen. This is not simply a plant wearing out. In the 1950s, plant scientists, including A. Carl Leopold in the United States, reported that if you keep removing the flowers and young pods from a soybean plant, the plant stays green and alive for much longer. So the developing seeds seem to speed the end of the plant. Scientists have two main ideas about why. Some think the seeds pull so much food and minerals out of the plant that nothing is left to keep the leaves going. Others think the seeds send a chemical signal that switches on the ageing of the whole plant. Probably both happen, and the balance differs from plant to plant.
examples: A marigold that is deadheaded, with the old flowers pinched off, keeps flowering for longer than one left to make seeds.
A soybean plant with the pods removed stays green long after untouched plants have died.
A banana stem, after fruiting, dies back, while new shoots at the base carry on.
explanations.art: Two soybean plants. One covered in pods has yellow leaves. One with the pods removed is still green and has new flowers.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour the food-drain idea
perspectives.explanation: The seeds are a big sink for nitrogen and sugar. The plant pulls everything out of the leaves to fill them, and the leaves, left empty, yellow and drop. Plants that cannot get more food from the soil run out first.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour the signal idea
perspectives.explanation: Developing seeds make a chemical message that tells the leaves to start senescence, even if food is still available. Some plants die after seeding even when they are well fed, which fits a signal.

explanations.concept: Annual, biennial and perennial: three ways to spend a life
explanations.definition: An annual finishes its life cycle in one year or less. A biennial takes two years, with leaves and food storage in the first year and flowers in the second. A perennial lives for many years and flowers in many seasons.
explanations.description: Moong, rice, palak, coriander and marigold are annuals. Carrot, beetroot, cabbage and onion are biennials. In the first year a biennial makes leaves and stores food in a swollen root or bulb. In the second year they use that stored food to send up a flower stalk, set seed and die. We usually eat them in their first year, before they flower. Mango, neem, coconut and banyan are perennials. The groups are not fixed. A tomato plant is a perennial in the tropics but is grown as an annual because the plant gets diseased with age. A chilli plant can live for several years if looked after. A castor plant grows as a small annual in a field but can become a small tree in a warm place. So length of life depends on the place and the care as well as on the kind of plant.
examples: Annual: moong, rice, wheat, palak and marigold.
Biennial: carrot, beetroot, cabbage and onion, which flower in their second year.
Perennial: mango, neem, banyan, coconut, hibiscus and tulsi.
explanations.art: Three rows on a timeline. An annual plant from seed to seed in one year, a carrot over two years, and a mango tree over many years.

explanations.concept: One big flowering or many small ones
explanations.definition: Some plants flower only once in a lifetime and then die. Scientists call them monocarpic. Others flower in many seasons. Scientists call them polycarpic.
explanations.description: A moong plant flowers for a few weeks and dies, so moong is monocarpic. A mango tree flowers every year for decades, so mango is polycarpic. Some long-lived plants wait for years, flower once and then die. An agave, the century plant, grows a rosette of thick leaves for ten to thirty years, then sends up a tall flower stalk and dies. The Mizoram bamboo and the talipot palm do the same. Each plant makes a choice, in the way that every living thing has to, between spending their energy on growing, which keeps the plant alive, and on seeds, which make new plants. A plant that flowers many times spreads their effort over the years. A plant that flowers once puts everything into one big bet. Banana is a mix. Each banana stem flowers once and dies, but the clump sends up new stems through suckers and carries on. Other living things make the same choice. Pacific salmon swim upstream, spawn once and die.
examples: Monocarpic: moong, rice, sunflower, agave, talipot palm and the Mizoram bamboo.
Polycarpic: mango, neem, coconut, banyan and peepal.
A banana stem flowers once, but the clump lives on through suckers.
explanations.art: An agave plant with a tall flower stalk, next to a mango tree with flowers and fruit and a timeline showing one flowering and many flowerings.

explanations.concept: Saving up for the second year
explanations.definition: Many plants swell a root, stem or bulb to store food for a time when they cannot make it. The plant uses the stored food to restart after the dry or cold season. We eat many of these stores.
explanations.description: A carrot is a swollen root. Beetroot is another one. A potato is a swollen underground stem, an onion is a bulb made of thick leaf bases, and ginger and turmeric are rhizomes, which are thick underground stems that grow sideways. All of these are savings. The plant makes sugar in the leaves in the good season and packs it away as starch. When the dry or cold season ends, the plant spends the savings to grow shoots fast, before there are leaves to make new food. If you put the top of a carrot in a saucer of water, feathery leaves sprout from it, living on the food in the carrot. The leaves cannot make a new carrot, but it shows what the carrot is for. We eat the savings of the plant. Seeds are another kind of savings, packed for the plant's young.
examples: Put the cut top of a carrot in water and it grows green leaves using the stored food.
A forgotten potato in a dark cupboard grows long pale shoots from the eyes.
Ginger and turmeric pieces left in a damp place put out buds and roots.
explanations.art: A carrot, a potato, a ginger root and an onion, each with a green shoot growing, and a small arrow from the food store to the shoot.

explanations.concept: How plants tell the season: day length
explanations.definition: Many plants measure the length of the night to tell the season. Short-day plants flower when nights are long. Long-day plants flower when nights are short. Day-neutral plants ignore day length.
explanations.description: Near the equator, the day length changes little through the year, but it changes enough for many plants to feel. In many parts of India, traditional kinds of rice are short-day plants. They flower when the nights become longer after the monsoon, whenever they were sown. Many modern kinds of rice are bred to be less sensitive, so that farmers can grow them in several seasons. Chrysanthemums are short-day plants, and flower growers cover the plants with dark cloth or add lamps at night to make them flower in time for a festival. Palak, coriander and lettuce are long-day plants. When the days grow long and hot, they send up a flower stalk, and the leaves turn bitter. Gardeners call this bolting. Tomato, cucumber and many beans are day-neutral. They flower when they are big enough. A plant measures the night with a clock inside the leaves. The leaves then send a message up the stem to the buds.
examples: Traditional rice flowers when the nights lengthen after the monsoon.
Coriander and palak bolt in the long, hot days of summer.
Flower growers cover chrysanthemums with dark cloth to bring on blooms for a festival.
explanations.art: Three plants side by side under a long day, a short day and a lamp at night, with flower buds on some and none on others.

explanations.concept: Remembering winter: flowering after a cold spell
explanations.definition: Some plants need a spell of cold before they will flower. The cold tells them that winter has passed. Scientists call this vernalisation. The plant remembers the cold for weeks.
explanations.description: In the 1910s, a German scientist, Gustav Gassner, showed that winter cereals, which are sown in autumn, flower only if the seed or seedling has been through cold. A seed that was kept warm made leaves but no flower stalk. If a plant flowered at the first warm day of autumn, the winter would kill the flowers. So the plant waits for a sign. What is remarkable is that the plant remembers the cold after it has gone. A small plant used in labs, a relative of mustard, holds the memory of winter in a gene that is switched off by chemical marks while the cold lasts. Caroline Dean, a British plant scientist, and her team have spent years finding how the plant's cells keep this memory. Apples, tulips and many hill flowers need winter chill. A mango tree in some places needs a cool, dry spell to flower.
examples: Tulip bulbs sold in warm countries are kept in cold storage first, so that they will flower.
Apple trees in Kashmir and Himachal need a cold winter to flower well.
In some places, mango trees flower after a cool dry spell.
explanations.art: A bulb under snow, then the same bulb sprouting in spring, with a thermometer showing cold and warm.

explanations.concept: Ferns: a life cycle with two bodies
explanations.definition: A fern grows from a spore, not a seed. The spore grows into a tiny, flat, heart-shaped plant, which makes eggs and sperm. The sperm swim to the egg through a film of water, and the fertilised egg grows into a new fern.
explanations.description: Turn over a fern leaf and look for rows of brown dots. These are clusters of spore cases. When they are ripe, they fling out spores like dust. A spore that lands on damp soil grows into a tiny green heart, only a few millimetres wide, called a prothallus. This is a separate small plant. The tiny plant makes eggs and sperm. When the soil is wet, the sperm swim to the eggs, so ferns need damp places. The egg grows into a baby fern, and the heart-shaped plant withers away. So a fern's life cycle has two different bodies, the big fern that makes spores and the tiny heart that makes eggs and sperm. Flowering plants have the same two stages, but the second one is hidden. A grain of pollen is the tiny male stage, and the seed-start inside the flower holds the tiny female stage. Mosses also use spores.
examples: Brown dots on the underside of a fern frond are spore cases.
A fern in a damp corner of a wall puts up fronds from a creeping rhizome.
A moss capsule on a thin stalk releases spores.
explanations.art: A ring with four pictures: a big fern with spore dots, a spore, a tiny heart-shaped plant on damp soil, and a baby fern growing from the heart.

explanations.concept: Copies and variety: cuttings, grafts and seedless fruit
explanations.definition: A plant grown from a cutting, a sucker or a graft is a clone, an exact copy of the parent. A plant grown from a seed gets instructions from two parents, so the new plant is a little different.
explanations.description: A farmer who wants every mango tree to bear the same sweet mangoes cannot plant stones, because each stone grows into a different tree. Instead the farmer grafts a twig from a good tree onto a young rooted plant. The twig grows into a branch that bears the same mangoes as its parent. Most Alphonso trees are grafts. Bananas we eat are seedless. They cannot make seeds, so every banana plant comes from a sucker or from a lab-grown cutting. Copies are quick and sure, and they keep the fruit the same. But copies have no variety. If a disease can harm one plant of that kind, it can harm all of them. Seeds, in contrast, mix instructions from two parents, and in a field of seedlings there are always some that cope with a new disease or a new climate. Variety is a plant's insurance.
examples: A money plant cutting rooted in water becomes a clone of the vine.
A grafted mango tree bears fruit in three to five years, which is sooner than a tree grown from a stone.
All the bananas of one kind in a plantation are clones from suckers.
explanations.art: A mango twig being tied onto a young mango stem, and next to it a mango tree grown from a stone with different-looking fruit.

explanations.concept: How old can a plant be?
explanations.description: Some plants live a very long time. A bristlecone pine in California is reported to be about 4,800 years old. The Sri Maha Bodhi, a peepal tree in Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, is said to have been planted in 288 BCE, which would make the tree more than 2,000 years old. A grove of quaking aspen trees in Utah called Pando is made of tens of thousands of trunks, all shoots of one root system, and the age of Pando is estimated at many thousands of years, though scientists disagree about how many. A clump of bamboo or banana can be older than any one stem in it. So the age of a plant depends on what you count: one trunk, or the whole living clone. Scientists also argue about whether trees age as animals do.
examples: A bristlecone pine in the dry mountains of California is reported to be about 4,800 years old.
The Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Sri Lanka is said to be planted in 288 BCE.
A banyan, such as the Great Banyan near Kolkata, spreads by roots hanging from the branches, and the original trunk can be replaced.
explanations.art: A twisted old pine on a dry mountain slope, a wide banyan with hanging roots, and a grove of aspen trunks joined by one root, shown on a long timeline.

perspectives.explanation: Many old trees show very little weakening with age. They keep growing and making seeds, and they die from accidents such as storms, fire, fungus or drought. On this view some trees show almost no ageing.
Big old trees do decline. They have more dead wood, rot in the centre, and carry a huge weight to feed, so they grow more slowly and are easier to kill. They simply decline very slowly.

explanations.concept: Tree rings: a diary in wood
explanations.definition: In places with a wet and a dry season, or a warm and a cold one, a tree grows fast in the good season and slowly in the poor one. This leaves a ring of wood for each year. Counting rings counts years, and the width of each ring records how good the year was.
explanations.description: Cut across a branch and you see a pattern of pale and dark circles. The pale wood grows in the good season, when there is rain, and the dark band grows in the dry or cold time. One pale and dark pair is one year. A wide ring means a good year with plenty of rain. A narrow ring means a hard year. Because the weather pattern is shared by all trees in a region, a dry year shows up as a narrow ring in every tree. Scientists match the patterns in living trees and old beams to read the weather of the past. Indian scientists have used the rings of teak trees to work out the monsoon rains of past centuries. Not every tree makes clear rings. Trees in places with no seasons may not.
examples: A log of teak or neem has clear rings from the dry and wet seasons.
A tree with 30 rings is about 30 years old.
A very narrow ring marks a drought year in the whole area.
explanations.art: A cut log with rings, with a few labelled: wide ring, good rain year; narrow ring, drought year; and the bark at the edge.

agreed.text: Ripe fruit give off ethylene, a gas that speeds the ripening of fruit nearby.
agreed.evidence: Fruit sealed in a bag with a ripe banana ripen sooner than fruit sealed alone. Scientists can measure the gas, and they have found the receptors that sense it.

agreed.text: A fruit ripens by changes inside it: starch becomes sugar, the walls loosen, the green fades, acids fall and scents are made.
agreed.evidence: These changes have been measured in many fruits, and the enzymes that cause them have been identified.

agreed.text: A leaf turning yellow is being taken apart in order, with useful materials moved to other parts of the plant.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have tracked nitrogen out of ageing leaves and into seeds and stems, and have found genes that switch the process on.

agreed.text: Many plants measure the length of the night, or a spell of cold, to decide when to flower.
agreed.evidence: Experiments in which a brief light is flashed in a long night, or a plant is chilled, change when the plant flowers.

agreed.text: Ferns reproduce with spores, and the spore grows into a tiny separate plant that makes eggs and sperm.
agreed.evidence: You can see this under a hand lens on damp soil a few weeks after sowing spores. Scientists described the whole cycle in the 1800s.

agreed.text: Plants grown from cuttings or grafts are copies, and plants grown from seed vary.
agreed.evidence: A row of grafted mango trees bear the same fruit, but a row of trees grown from stones bear different ones.

challenging.claim: Fruit ripen only because of the sun's heat.
challenging.for: Fruit on a tree ripen in warm weather, and ripening is slow in cold. Heat does speed up the process.
challenging.against: A banana picked green ripens in a dark cupboard. A mango in a bag with a ripe banana ripens faster than one in the sun alone. In the 1920s, growers who heated lemons with kerosene stoves thought the heat coloured the lemons. The fumes of the stove were the cause, not the heat.

challenging.claim: Every kind of fruit goes on ripening after it is picked.
challenging.for: Mangoes, bananas, papayas and tomatoes do ripen after picking, so it seems true of fruit in general.
challenging.against: Grapes, oranges, pineapples, strawberries and watermelons are picked ripe and do not get sweeter later. A green grape put in a bag with a banana stays sour.

challenging.claim: An annual plant dies after seeding simply from being worn out.
challenging.for: A moong plant looks tired at the end, with yellow leaves and dry stems. The plant has used up a lot of food.
challenging.against: In soybean, taking off the flowers and young pods keeps the plant green and alive for much longer. So the seeds seem to take part in ending the plant. The end of the plant is partly set off by the seeds.

challenging.claim: Ferns have seeds so tiny that nobody can see them, and people who carry fern seed become invisible.
challenging.who: Many people in Europe for hundreds of years. Shakespeare has a character joke about it in a play.
challenging.for: Ferns never show flowers or fruit, yet new ferns keep appearing, so people guessed there were hidden seeds.
challenging.against: In the 1800s, scientists with microscopes saw that the brown dust under a fern leaf is spores, not seeds, and that spores grow into a tiny heart-shaped plant. The fern has no flowers or seeds at all.

challenging.claim: A plant can pass on to their seeds what they learned in their own lifetime, so cold-treated wheat gives seeds that no longer need cold.
challenging.who: Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet agronomist with political power in the 1930s and 1940s.
challenging.for: Cold treatment of winter wheat really does change when the plant flowers, and some plants do pass on small chemical marks to the next generation.
challenging.against: Careful experiments showed that the seeds of cold-treated plants still need the cold. The strong claim was false, and it did great harm. Lysenko's power was used against geneticists. Nikolai Vavilov, who built a great seed collection, died in prison in 1943.

big_questions.q: A ripe banana changes a raw mango without touching it. What else in the world changes something without touching it?
big_questions.hint: Think about smell, sound, light and warmth.

big_questions.q: A moong plant dies as the seeds ripen. Is dying part of the plan, or a failure?
big_questions.hint: What happens to the leaves' materials when a leaf yellows?

big_questions.q: Every banana stem lives about a year, yet a banana clump can go on for decades. Which one is the plant: the stem or the clump?
big_questions.hint: Where does the new stem come from? What would you say if the clump is 50 years old?

big_questions.q: A fern has a big body at one time of life and a tiny body at another. Which one is the real fern?
big_questions.hint: Is a caterpillar the real butterfly? Or is it the other way round?

big_questions.q: Bristlecone pines grow very slowly in poor soil and live for thousands of years. What do you think slow growth buys them?
big_questions.hint: Think about wood that is dense, and about rot and insects.

big_questions.q: Almost every banana we eat is a copy of one kind. What would we lose if that kind caught a disease, and what could we do?
big_questions.hint: Why do seeds give variety? Why can seedless bananas not use it?

big_questions.q: If trees keep a diary in their rings, what can that diary tell us that no book can?
big_questions.hint: A tree 300 years old saw the rains of 300 years. Who wrote those down?

big_questions.q: A bamboo clump 'waits' 48 years to flower. Is waiting without a brain still waiting?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to see in a bamboo to say that they are counting?

story.title: Four Days to Sunday
story.note: Anjana, her family and the mango cart are made up. The science is real. A ripe banana gives off ethylene, which speeds the ripening of raw mangoes nearby. Fruit also need fresh air, and a sealed box can spoil them. Ripening mangoes in rice or straw is a real traditional method. Calcium carbide is not allowed for ripening fruit in India. The times in the story are typical, but real ripening depends on the fruit and the weather.
text: Anjana's uncle sold mangoes from a handcart near the temple in Thrissur. In the mango season, the cart was heaped high with small, sweet moovandan mangoes. But this year the mangoes ripened late. On Wednesday morning, every mango on the cart was still as hard and green as a stone.

That morning, a woman in a bright cotton sari stopped at the cart. 'My daughter's wedding is on Sunday,' she said. 'I need forty ripe mangoes for the pulissery. Can you have them ready by Saturday night?' Anjana's uncle, Vinod, looked at his green heap. He did not want to lose the order. 'Saturday night,' he said. 'Yes.' After the woman had gone, he rubbed his forehead. Nobody could ripen forty mangoes in three days.

A woman from the next stall had been listening. 'Easy,' she said. She held out a paper packet of small grey stones. 'Put these in the box with the mangoes. By morning, they will be yellow.' Anjana knew the grey stones. They were called carbide. Her teacher, Rekha Madam, had told the class that carbide is not allowed for ripening fruit, because it can leave harmful dirt on the skin. 'No,' said Anjana. 'Not on our cart.' Uncle Vinod looked at her, and then at the packet. 'No,' he said, a little slowly. 'Not on my cart.'

Anjana's grandmother, Ammamma, was sitting on a stool beside the cart, sorting mangoes. 'In my village,' she said, 'we buried raw mangoes in a basket of rice and put a cloth over the top. In four or five days, they came out yellow.' 'Why does the rice help?' asked Anjana. Ammamma laughed. 'The rice never told me.'

But Anjana had an idea, and it came from school. Last week, Rekha Madam had put a hard green mango in a paper bag with a very ripe banana. She had put another in a bag alone. After four days, the mango with the banana was soft and yellow, and the other was still firm. 'The two never touched,' Madam had said. 'A ripe fruit gives out a gas that you cannot see. It is called ethylene. Raw fruit nearby can sense it, and they start to ripen too. The bag keeps the gas close.'

'Bananas,' said Anjana. 'We need very ripe bananas.' By evening, Uncle Vinod had bought two dozen spotty bananas from the market, at half the usual price, because they were so ripe. They packed the forty mangoes into a big cardboard carton and tucked a banana in among them. Then Uncle Vinod sealed the whole carton with brown tape, all the way around, to keep the gas in. 'Tight as a drum,' he said proudly.

On Thursday evening, they peeped through a corner. Nothing had changed. The mangoes were still hard. On Friday morning, Anjana opened the carton, and a sour smell rolled out, like old curd. A few of the bananas had turned black and soft. Some of the mangoes had a dull yellow patch, and the rest were still green. 'It has gone wrong,' said Uncle Vinod. 'Maybe we should have used the stones.' Anjana did not answer. She was thinking.

She remembered the bags at school. Every morning, Rekha Madam had opened them for a minute and flapped them. 'Why?' someone had asked. 'Because fruit breathe,' said Madam. 'They need fresh air. Shut in a small space for too long, they use up the air, and they spoil instead of ripening.'

'Uncle,' said Anjana, 'we sealed them too tightly. They have no air.' 'But you said the bag keeps the gas in,' said her uncle. 'It does,' said Anjana. 'We need to keep the gas in and let the air in. Both.' Uncle Vinod scratched his head. 'How can you do both?'

Anjana thought of Ammamma's basket of rice. Rice is full of tiny gaps. Gas can stay among the grains, and air can seep in through them. 'We do not need to close it like a drum,' she said. 'We need to close it like a basket with a cloth.'

They peeled off the tape. They threw out the black bananas and put in fresh ripe ones. They set the mangoes in a single layer, with a banana close to every few. They laid a thick cloth loosely over the top. And every morning and every evening, they lifted the cloth for a minute and fanned fresh air in.

On Friday night, the first mangoes began to smell sweet. On Saturday morning, a third of them were yellow. By Saturday afternoon, Anjana pressed one with her thumb, and it gave softly. 'Warm and soft,' she said. They sorted them. Thirty-six mangoes were ready, soft, yellow and fragrant. Four were still hard.

The woman came on Saturday evening. She pressed a mango herself, and smelled it, and smiled. 'Thirty-six will do,' she said. 'The rest I can use for pickle.' She counted out the money. Uncle Vinod's hand shook a little as he took it.

Later, the woman from the next stall came by. She looked at the carton, at the cloth and at the heap of black bananas. 'How did you do it without stones?' she asked. 'Bananas,' said Anjana. 'And fresh air.' 'Bananas?' said the woman, and shook her head. 'Next time, bring your own bananas,' said Uncle Vinod, and for the first time that week, he laughed.

That night, Anjana sat with Ammamma on the doorstep. 'So the rice was doing the work all along,' she said. 'Rice, straw and bananas,' said Ammamma. 'People knew how before they knew why.' 'And now we know why,' said Anjana. 'One fruit tells the others. Without touching.' Ammamma looked at the carton in the dark. 'Then the question is not only how a fruit ripens,' she said. 'It is how a fruit speaks.'
story.epiphany: A ripe fruit sends out a gas that tells raw fruit nearby to ripen. The gas works best when kept close, but ripening fruit also need fresh air.

How does a ripe banana change a raw mango that it never touches?

games.title: One Season or Many? Guess how a plant spends a life
games.context: This is a guessing game about plant lives. Each card names a plant with a clue. You guess if the plant flowers in one season or many, and how long the plant lives.

setup.art: Twenty plant cards in a pile and a row of seven answer tokens for each player, two for the season and five for the time.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and one set of seven tokens for each player.

setup.art: A reader holding up the front of a card that says Moong, while players each put two tokens face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front of a card. Everyone picks two tokens.

setup.art: Players turning over their tokens together while the reader reads the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. The reader reads the back. Score your points.

printables.title: 20 plant cards. A plant with a clue is on the front, and the answer is on the back

items.f: Moong. A small bean plant, grown in pots and fields. Clue: the pods turn black when ripe.
items.b: ONE SEASON. Flowers at about 5 weeks and dies when the pods ripen. TIME: a year or less, about 3 months.

items.f: Carrot. We eat the orange root. Clue: market carrots are picked before they flower.
items.b: ONE SEASON, but in the second year. The first year makes leaves and a fat root. The second year makes the flower and seeds. TIME: two years.

items.f: Rice. A grass grown in wet fields. Clue: the crop is harvested after the grain turns golden.
items.b: ONE SEASON. About 4 to 6 months from seed to grain. TIME: a year or less.

items.f: Marigold. A garland flower sold by the kilo. Clue: gardeners pinch off the old flowers.
items.b: ONE SEASON. A marigold flowers for many weeks, then makes seeds and dies. Pinching old flowers keeps the plant flowering longer. TIME: a year or less.

items.f: Sunflower. A tall plant with a huge flower head. Clue: the head is full of seeds when it dries.
items.b: ONE SEASON. About 3 to 4 months from seed to seed. TIME: a year or less.

items.f: Wheat. A grass grown for chapati flour. Clue: the crop is sown in the cool season and harvested in summer.
items.b: ONE SEASON. About 4 to 5 months from sowing to grain. TIME: a year or less.

items.f: Onion. We eat the bulb. Clue: farmers collect onion seeds from bulbs left to grow another year.
items.b: ONE SEASON, in the second year. An onion is a biennial. TIME: two years.

items.f: A banana stem. The thick green trunk is really leaf bases. Clue: after the bunch is cut, the stem is cut down.
items.b: ONE SEASON for each stem. A stem flowers once, makes one bunch and dies. New stems grow from suckers. TIME: about a year for each stem.

items.f: Papaya. A fast-growing fruit plant. Clue: papaya gives fruit in less than a year, but old plants fruit poorly.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A papaya plant fruits for about 3 to 4 years, then is replaced. TIME: a few years.

items.f: Tulsi. A holy basil kept in many courtyards. Clue: the plant is a woody little bush that keeps flowering.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A tulsi bush flowers again and again, and with care lives a few years. TIME: a few years.

items.f: Sugarcane. A tall grass grown for juice and jaggery. Clue: after cutting, the stumps sprout again.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. Cane regrows from the stumps for a few harvests, but farmers replant every few years. TIME: a few years.

items.f: Coconut palm. A tall tree on the coast. Clue: the nuts hang in bunches, all year round.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A palm starts to bear nuts at about 5 to 10 years and can live for 60 years or more. TIME: decades.

items.f: Mango tree. The king of fruits. Clue: a tree grown from a graft fruits in 3 to 5 years.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A mango tree can live for more than a hundred years, and some are said to be much older. TIME: centuries or more.

items.f: Neem. A bitter-leafed tree beside many roads. Clue: neem flowers every spring and drops seeds in the monsoon.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A neem tree can live for well over a hundred years. TIME: centuries or more.

items.f: Banyan. A huge tree with roots hanging from the branches. Clue: the Great Banyan near Kolkata is said to be about 250 years old.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A banyan fruits year after year and can live for centuries. TIME: centuries or more.

items.f: Peepal. A tree often planted near temples. Clue: the Sri Maha Bodhi in Sri Lanka is said to have been planted in 288 BCE.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. A peepal can live for centuries, and the Sri Maha Bodhi is said to be more than 2,000 years old. TIME: centuries or more.

items.f: Bamboo of Mizoram. A giant grass. Clue: the whole forest flowers on the same year, then dies.
items.b: ONE SEASON. This bamboo waits about 48 years, flowers all together and dies. TIME: decades.

items.f: Agave. A spiky rosette of thick leaves, also called the century plant. Clue: an agave sends up a flower stalk taller than a house.
items.b: ONE SEASON. An agave grows for about 10 to 30 years, flowers once and dies, leaving suckers. TIME: decades.

items.f: Talipot palm. A giant palm with the biggest flower cluster of any plant. Clue: the palm makes the flower cluster only once.
items.b: ONE SEASON. A talipot palm waits more than 30 years, flowers once and dies. TIME: decades.

items.f: Bristlecone pine. A twisted pine of dry mountains in California. Clue: the pine grows very slowly, with dense wood.
items.b: MANY SEASONS. Some bristlecone pines are reported to be about 4,800 years old. TIME: centuries or more.

printables.title: 7 answer tokens for each player, to cut out: ONE SEASON, MANY SEASONS, A YEAR OR LESS, TWO YEARS, A FEW YEARS, DECADES, CENTURIES OR MORE
A score sheet with a row for each player
items: Player | Points after cards 1 to 10 | Points after cards 11 to 20 | Total

rules: Cut out the 20 cards. Each player cuts out one set of the seven tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
In each round, the reader turns over the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every player secretly picks one season token, ONE SEASON or MANY SEASONS, and one time token, and puts both face down.
ONE SEASON means that the plant flowers in just one season of the plant's life, then dies. MANY SEASONS means that the plant flowers in many seasons.
The time tokens are how long the plant lives: a year or less, two years, a few years, decades, or centuries or more. A few years means about 3 to 10 years. Decades means 10 to 99 years.

Everyone turns their tokens over together. The reader reads the back. A right season token wins 1 point. A right time token wins 1 point. Both right wins 1 more point, so a card is worth up to 3 points.
The job of reader passes to the next player after each round. After all 20 cards, the player with the most points wins. Ties share the win.
Playing alone: pick your tokens for each card before you read the back. Try to score 40 or more out of 60.

No printer? Write each plant name and clue on a slip of paper. A parent can read the back from the app. Write the seven token words on small pieces of paper. With 2 to 4 players the reader changes each round, so everyone can play.

flow.context: This is the first step of One Season or Many. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. 2. Give each player a set of seven tokens. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
flow.say: Plants live their lives in different ways. Some flower once and die. Some flower year after year. We will guess for twenty plants.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Mix the cards. Take your seven tokens.

flow.context: In this step you play one practice round to learn the game.
flow.do: Play one practice round with the moong card. The reader reads the front. Each player picks two tokens. Then the reader reads the back.
flow.say: A moong plant makes pods and the pods turn black. Does the plant flower in one season or many? How long does it live? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Read the moong card. Pick two tokens. Say why.

ask.q: What clue on the card helped you decide?
good: The pods turn black, so the plant is finished.
It makes seeds, then dies.
It is a small bean plant.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Let your child say the reason first, then read the back. Note how many points your child scored.

flow.context: In this step you play the first half of the game.
flow.do: Play cards 2 to 10. After each round, add the points to the score sheet. Say one new thing you learned from the back of each card.
flow.say: Pick your tokens. Turn them over together. What did you guess? What was the answer? What surprised you?
flow.kid: Play the next nine cards. Pick your tokens. Check the back.

check.q: A plant flowers in only one season of a lifetime and dies, but it takes 48 years to get there. Which tokens fit?
options: ONE SEASON and DECADES
MANY SEASONS and DECADES
ONE SEASON and A YEAR OR LESS
check.why: ONE SEASON means that the plant flowers once and then dies. DECADES means that the plant lives between 10 and 99 years. A plant that waits 48 years and flowers once fits both.

flow.context: In this step you play the second half of the game and count the scores.
flow.do: Play cards 11 to 20. Add up the scores.
flow.say: Keep going. Which kinds of plants live longest? Which kinds flower only once?
flow.kid: Play the last ten cards. Add up your points.

flow.context: In this step you sort the cards and look for patterns.
flow.do: Lay out all the cards in order of how long the plant lives. Ask which plants flower only once, and what they have in common.
flow.say: Look at the plants that flower only once. Some are short-lived and some wait for decades. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Sort the cards by how long each plant lives. Which plants flower only once?

ask.q: What do the plants that flower once have in common?
good: They put everything into one big flowering.
They die after making seeds.
Some are small and quick, and some wait a long time.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer here. The stem flowers once and the clump flowers many times, and a plant can be described either way.
flow.think: A banana stem flowers once, but the banana clump goes on. So is a banana a plant that flowers once, or many times?

games.title: Ripen After Picking? Sort the fruit
games.context: This is a sorting game. Some fruit keep ripening after they are picked, and some do not. Players decide which, and explain why.

setup.art: Two paper mats on a table, one labelled KEEPS RIPENING and one labelled DOES NOT, with a pile of fruit cards between them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the two mats. Put the 20 fruit cards in a pile with the names facing up.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says Banana on the mat labelled KEEPS RIPENING while another player says I disagree.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card, choose a mat and say why. Others can say I disagree.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the answer, with a point token beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. A right answer with a reason wins a point.

printables.title: 20 fruit cards. A fruit name is on the front, and the answer is on the back

items.f: Papaya
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A papaya that is turning yellow at one end ripens fully on the shelf.

items.f: Tomato
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A tomato picked pale ripens to red on a warm shelf.

items.f: Guava
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A hard green guava softens and gets sweeter after picking.

items.f: Apple
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. An apple gives off a lot of ethylene and ripens fruit around it.

items.f: Sapota (chikoo)
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A hard sapota must be left to soften before it is sweet.

items.f: Jackfruit
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A jackfruit cut early softens and sweetens as it sits.

items.f: Avocado
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. An avocado stays hard on the tree and ripens only after it is picked.

items.f: Pear
items.b: KEEPS RIPENING. A pear picked hard ripens on the shelf.

items.f: Grapes
items.b: DOES NOT. Grapes are picked ripe. A sour grape stays sour.

items.f: Orange
items.b: DOES NOT. Oranges are picked ripe and do not get sweeter off the tree.

items.f: Sweet lime (mosambi)
items.b: DOES NOT. A mosambi is picked when it is ready and will not sweeten later.

items.f: Lemon
items.b: DOES NOT. A lemon only turns yellow off the tree. It does not get less sour.

items.f: Pineapple
items.b: DOES NOT. A pineapple is picked ripe. Its sugar does not rise after picking.

items.f: Strawberry
items.b: DOES NOT. Strawberries are picked fully red and do not get sweeter later.

items.f: Watermelon
items.b: DOES NOT. A watermelon is picked ripe and does not ripen more on a shelf.

items.f: Cucumber
items.b: DOES NOT. A cucumber does not ripen on the shelf. It only ages.

items.f: Pomegranate
items.b: DOES NOT. A pomegranate is picked ripe and does not ripen more later.

items.f: Lychee
items.b: DOES NOT. Lychees are picked ripe and do not get sweeter after picking.

rules: Cut out the 20 cards and the two mats. Put the cards in a pile with the fruit names facing up.
Take turns to take the top card and say which mat it goes on, and why. You win 1 point for the right mat.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ripen After Picking. You lay out the cards and the mats.
flow.do: Lay out the two mats and the cards. Look through all the fruit names together.
flow.say: Some fruit, picked green, will ripen on your shelf. Others will not. Today you decide which are which.
flow.kid: Lay out the mats. Read the fruit names.

flow.context: In this step you play a practice round with two fruit.
flow.do: Play a practice round with banana and grapes. Put each on a mat and give a reason.
flow.say: A green banana will turn yellow on the shelf. What about a sour green grape? Which mat does each go on? Why?
flow.kid: Put banana and grapes on mats. Say why.

ask.q: Why might a grape not ripen more after it is picked?
good: It is picked ripe already.
It does not make the ripening gas.
A grape only ripens on the vine.

flow.parent: Fruit that keep ripening after picking are called climacteric. They make a burst of ethylene as they ripen. Others, such as grapes, are non-climacteric and ripen only on the plant.

flow.context: In this step you play the sorting game.
flow.do: Play the game by the rules. After each card, say the answer and one thing the fruit might have in common with the ones on the same mat.
flow.say: Take a card. Choose a mat. Say why. Does anyone disagree? Now let's check the back.
flow.kid: Take a card. Choose a mat. Say why. Check the back.

check.q: A shopper picks a sour green pineapple, hoping it will sweeten on the shelf. What will probably happen?
options: It will stay about as sour, because pineapples do not sweeten after picking
It will turn sweet in two days
It will turn into a banana
check.why: Pineapples are non-climacteric. They are picked ripe and do not get sweeter later. A banana, a mango or a tomato would ripen on the shelf.

flow.context: In this step you look for patterns in the sorted fruit.
flow.do: Look at the fruit on each mat. Ask what the fruit on the KEEPS RIPENING mat have in common.
flow.say: Look at the fruit on the first mat. What do you notice? Which fruit would you put in a bag with a hard mango?
flow.kid: Look at the fruit on the first mat. What do they have in common?
flow.parent: Many of the fruit that keep ripening are soft and sweet, with a strong smell. Those fruit also give off a lot of ethylene, so they make good helpers in a ripening bag.
flow.think: If you wanted to ripen a hard avocado, which fruit would you put in the bag with it?

items.p: Meena puts a hard green papaya in a paper bag with a very ripe banana. The papaya ripens sooner than a papaya left alone. What does the banana give off that helps the papaya ripen?
items.why: A ripe banana gives off ethylene, a gas that raw fruit nearby can sense. It tells them to start ripening. Picking 'heat' is a common guess, but a banana gives off almost no heat. Picking 'sugar' mixes up what is inside the banana with what leaves it.

items.p: A sour green grape put in a bag with a ripe banana will slowly turn sweet.
items.why: False. Grapes are picked ripe, and they do not get sweeter after picking. Fruit such as bananas, mangoes and tomatoes keep ripening after picking, but grapes, oranges and pineapples do not.

items.p: Why does a mango taste sweeter when it is ripe than when it is raw?
opts: Enzymes cut the stored starch into sugar
The mango takes in sugar from the air
The skin makes the inside sweeter
Water inside the mango turns into sugar
items.why: A raw mango stores starch. When it ripens, enzymes cut the starch into sugar, and the acids fall, so the fruit tastes sweeter. Picking 'from the air' is not right, because the fruit makes the change from its own stores.

items.p: As a fruit ripens, enzymes cut the stored ____ into sugar.
items.why: Raw fruit, such as a green banana, are full of starch. Ripening turns the starch into sugar, which is why a yellow banana is sweet and a green one is not.

items.p: Explain in two or three sentences why it helps a plant when their fruit turn soft, sweet and scented just when the seeds are ready.
items.a: A soft, sweet, scented fruit attracts animals such as birds, bats, monkeys and people. They eat the fruit and carry the seeds away, and drop them far from the parent plant. A hard sour green fruit stays untouched until the seeds are ready, so the plant keeps them safe.
items.why: A strong answer links the changes to the seeds. Ripeness is a signal that says the seeds are ready to be carried.

items.p: A shopkeeper packs ripening mangoes tightly in a sealed plastic box for several days. When he opens it, a sour smell rolls out and many mangoes are spoiled. What is the best explanation?
opts: Ripening fruit breathe, and in a sealed space the air runs low, so they spoil
Sealing fruit always makes them ripen faster
The box got too much light
items.why: Fruit breathe oxygen even while they ripen. In a sealed box the oxygen falls, and the fruit spoil instead of ripening. Picking 'sealing always speeds ripening' mixes up holding in the gas with shutting out the air.

items.p: Putting a hard green tomato in the fridge is a good way to make it ripen faster.
items.why: False. Ripening is chemistry, and it runs slowly in the cold. A fruit from a warm place can also be damaged by a long spell in the cold. Ripen the fruit on a warm shelf, and cool it afterwards if it is ripe.

items.p: Sort these fruit. Do they keep ripening after they are picked, or not?
items.why: Banana, mango and tomato make a burst of ethylene as they ripen, and they go on ripening after picking. Grapes, oranges and pineapples are picked ripe and do not get sweeter later.

items.p: A leaf on a plant turns yellow at the end of the growing season. What is the plant doing?
opts: Taking the leaf apart and moving useful materials into the stem, roots or seeds
Giving up on the leaf because the leaf is dirty
items.why: A leaf is taken apart in order. The plant breaks down the green chlorophyll and moves the nitrogen and other useful materials out. The yellow substances were in the leaf all along and show once the green goes. Picking 'giving up' misses that the plant is saving all that can be saved.

items.p: Match each plant to the way they live.
pairs: flowers in one season and dies in under a year
stores food in year one and flowers in year two
flowers in many seasons for many years
waits for years, flowers once and dies
items.why: A moong plant is an annual. A carrot is a biennial. A mango is a perennial that flowers many times. An agave waits many years and flowers once.

items.p: Put these in order for a carrot plant, from first to last.
items: The seed sprouts and grows leaves
The root swells with stored food
In the second year, a flower stalk grows using the stored food
The flowers make seeds and the plant dies
items.why: In the first year, the carrot makes leaves and stores food in the root. In the second year, the plant spends that food to flower and make seeds. Then the plant dies.

items.p: Coriander and palak often send up flower stalks and turn bitter in summer. What is the best explanation?
opts: Long, hot days tell these plants that it is time to flower and make seed
They are tired of being picked
items.why: Palak and coriander are long-day plants. When days grow long and warm, they send up a flower stalk, which gardeners call bolting. Picking 'tired of being picked' puts the cause in the wrong place. The day length is the sign.

items.p: Three neighbours disagree about how to keep a bunch of palak fresh. Each gives advice.

views.says: Keep the palak in the fruit bowl, next to the ripe bananas, so you see it and use it.
Wrap the palak in a damp cloth and keep it in a box, away from the fruit bowl.
Seal the palak in a plastic bag in the fridge, so no air can reach it.

items.ask: Which advice would you follow? Give a reason from what you know about leaves and ripe fruit. Then say one thing another neighbour gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks Rukmini's plan. Ripe bananas give off ethylene, which makes leaves yellow sooner, so keeping the palak away from fruit helps. A damp cloth keeps the leaves from drying out. Hasan is right that the fridge slows ageing, but a sealed plastic bag can make leaves slimy. Sheela is right that the palak is more likely to be used if it is in sight, but the bananas shorten its life. A strong answer gives each plan its due.
items.why: Ethylene from ripe fruit pushes leaves to age. Cool, damp and airy storage keeps leaves fresh longest.

items.p: Draw the life cycle of a fern as a circle with four pictures: a big fern with spore dots, a spore, a tiny heart-shaped plant and a baby fern. Join them with arrows.
items.a: A circle of four pictures joined by arrows. A big fern with brown dots under its fronds leads to a spore. The spore leads to a tiny heart-shaped plant on damp soil. The heart-shaped plant leads to a baby fern, which grows into the big fern.
items.why: A fern has two bodies. The big fern makes spores, and the tiny heart-shaped plant makes eggs and sperm.
items.art: An empty circle with four boxes joined by arrows.

items.p: Which is the odd one out? Carrot, beetroot, onion, mango.
items.why: Carrot, beetroot and onion are biennials. They store food in the first year and flower in the second. A mango is a perennial tree that flowers in many seasons.

items.p: A farmer says, 'If I plant mango stones, I get a different tree each time. If I graft a twig from my best tree, I get a copy.' Explain why this happens.
items.a: A mango stone is a seed, and a seed gets instructions from two parents, so each seedling is a little different. A grafted twig is a piece of the best tree, so the new branch has exactly the same instructions and bears the same fruit.
items.why: A strong answer says that seeds mix instructions from two parents, and that a cutting or graft is a copy of one parent.

items.p: A banana stem flowers once, makes one bunch and dies. Yet a banana clump can go on for decades. How?
opts: New stems keep growing from suckers at the base
The roots die and grow again
items.why: Each banana stem lives about a year, but the clump sends up suckers, which become new stems. So the clump goes on while each stem has just one season. Picking 'seeds' is a common guess, but the bananas we eat are seedless.

items.p: Tulip bulbs sold in a warm country are kept in a cold store before they are planted. Why?
opts: Tulips need a spell of cold before they will flower
Cold keeps the bulbs from growing roots
items.why: Tulips need a winter chill, which tells the plant that winter has passed. A warm-country grower gives the chill in a cold store. Picking 'kills germs' sounds sensible but does not explain the flowering.

items.p: A tree that has 40 rings in a seasonal climate is about ____ years old.
items.why: In a place with a wet and a dry season, a tree usually adds one ring a year. So 40 rings means about 40 years. It is a good guess but not perfect, because some years can leave a missing or double ring.

items.p: In a year with very little rain, a tree in a seasonal climate usually makes a wider ring than in a wet year.
items.why: False. A tree grows more in a good year with plenty of water, so the ring is wider. A drought year leaves a narrow ring. Scientists use the widths to read the weather of the past.

items.p: Explain why pinching off the old flowers of a marigold can keep the plant flowering for longer.
items.a: A marigold that is left to make seeds spends its food on the seeds, and slows down once the seeds are filling. When the old flowers are pinched off, there are no seeds to fill, so the plant keeps making new flowers to try again.
items.why: A strong answer says that the seeds take the plant's food and signal the plant to slow down.

items.p: A fern spore contains a baby plant and a store of food, just like a seed.
items.why: False. A spore is a single tiny cell. The spore has no baby plant and no food store. The spore must land on damp ground and grow into a tiny heart-shaped plant, which then makes eggs and sperm.

items.p: Match each stage of a fern's life to its job.
pairs: lands on damp soil and grows into a tiny plant
grows into a big fern that makes spores
items.why: A fern's life cycle goes round with two bodies. The big fern makes the spores. The tiny heart makes the eggs and sperm.

items.p: Why do ferns usually live in damp, shady places?
opts: The sperm must swim through a film of water to reach the egg
Ferns make flowers in the dark
items.why: Fern sperm swim to the egg through a thin film of water, so ferns need damp places to reproduce. Picking 'dislike light' is a common idea. Many ferns do grow in sun if they have enough water.

items.p: Sort these new plants. Are they a clone of one parent, or grown from seed?
items: a money plant cutting rooted in water
a marigold grown from a seed
a mango tree grown from a stone
a wheat plant grown from a grain
items.why: Cuttings, grafts and suckers are pieces of one plant, so they are exact copies. Seeds mix instructions from two parents, so seedlings are all a little different.

items.p: Most bananas we eat are clones of just a few kinds. Why could one disease be a danger to all of them?
opts: All the plants are exact copies, so they share the same weakness
items.why: If every plant has the same instructions, a disease that can harm one can harm all. Seeds give variety, and in a field of seedlings some may resist the disease. Picking 'diseases like sweet fruit' misses the role of variety.

items.p: Flower growers in some places cover chrysanthemums with dark cloth in the evening, for part of the year. Why?
opts: Chrysanthemums flower when nights are long, so the cloth tricks them into thinking the night is long
items.why: Chrysanthemums are short-day plants. They flower when nights are long. Covering them in the evening makes a short day, which tells the plant to flower. Growers use this to time their blooms for a festival.

items.p: Tree scientists disagree about whether old trees age the way animals do. Three of them give their views.

views.says: Many old trees show little weakening. They keep growing and making seeds, and they die from accidents such as storms, fire and drought.
Big old trees do decline. They rot at the centre and grow more slowly, and they are easier to kill, though they decline very slowly.
It depends on the kind of tree. A short-lived tree may wear out. A bristlecone pine may hardly age at all.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Give a reason from what you know about trees. Then say what you would need to test it.
items.a: There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses facts such as that some trees keep making seeds into great age, and that big old trees can rot inside. It also says how to test the view, such as measuring the growth and seed output of trees of different ages. A strong answer gives each view its due.
items.why: The question is still debated. Different kinds of tree behave in different ways, and it is hard to follow a tree for centuries.

items.p: A traditional rice variety flowers when the nights grow longer after the monsoon. It is called a ____-day plant.
items.why: Short-day plants flower when the nights are long, which means the days are short. Many traditional rice varieties are like this. Many modern rice varieties are less sensitive.

items.p: A farmer wants every mango tree on the farm to bear the same sweet mangoes, and wants fruit as early as possible. What should the farmer plant, and why? Say one risk of this choice.
items.a: The farmer should buy grafted saplings of the best variety, not stones. A graft is a copy of a good tree and fruits in about three to five years, which is sooner than a tree grown from a stone. The risk is that all the trees are copies, so one disease could harm every tree.
items.why: A strong answer chooses grafts, gives the reason (a copy, and early fruit), and names the risk of having no variety.

items.p: Draw a tree trunk cut across, showing about 10 rings. Make one ring very narrow and one very wide. Label the narrow ring with a likely cause, and the wide ring with a likely cause.
items.a: A circle with about ten rings of different widths. The narrow ring is labelled drought or dry year. The wide ring is labelled good rain year.
items.why: A ring's width records how good the year was for the tree. Narrow means a hard year, and wide means a good year.
items.art: An empty circle for a tree trunk cut across.

items.p: A leaf still on a plant has a patch covered with black paper for a week. What will you most likely see when you take the paper off?
opts: The covered patch has turned yellow while the rest of the leaf is green
The covered patch is darker green
items.why: The covered patch could not make food, so the plant began taking that part of the leaf apart. The rest of the leaf, which had light, stayed green. Picking 'darker green' mixes up the effect of light with the effect of dark.

items.p: Growers thought that the heat from kerosene stoves coloured their lemons. To test this, scientists kept the ____ the same in every chamber and changed only the gas.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing. Keeping the temperature the same and changing only the gas showed that the gas, not the heat, made the lemons turn yellow.

items.p: In a sealed plant chamber on a space station, ethylene made by the plants builds up. What is the likely result, and what do the crew do?
opts: The plants age and drop leaves sooner, so the crew remove the gas
The plants grow faster, so the crew add more gas
The plants make flowers at once
items.why: Ethylene pushes leaves and fruit to age, so too much of it is harmful. In sealed chambers, the gas has to be removed. Picking 'grow faster' mixes up a ripening signal with a growth signal.

items.p: Many families in India have ripened mangoes in a basket of rice or straw for generations. Explain why this might work, using what you know about the ripening gas and warmth.
items.a: A heap of rice or straw holds the ethylene that the mangoes give off, so it stays close and builds up. The heap is also warm, and ripening is faster in warmth. Air can still seep in through the gaps. So the mangoes ripen together in a gentle, warm cloud of their own gas.
items.why: A strong answer links the heap to holding the gas, warmth and fresh air.

items.p: Why might a plant gain from taking leaves apart before dropping them?
opts: It saves the nitrogen and minerals for the seeds or for next season
It makes the leaf more colourful for visitors
It stops the roots from growing
items.why: Nitrogen and minerals are valuable, because the plant has had to gather them from the soil. Moving them out of the leaves before they fall lets the plant use them again. Picking 'colourful for visitors' is a guess, but yellow leaves are not meant to attract anyone.

items.p: In an experiment, a soybean plant that keeps the pods dies sooner than a plant whose flowers and pods are removed. Which idea does this best support?
opts: The developing seeds help to end the life of the plant
items.why: When the seeds are removed, the plant stays green for much longer. So the seeds seem to take part in ending the plant, either by drawing off the plant's food or by a chemical signal. Picking 'pods keep a plant alive' reads the result backwards.

items.p: Almost all the bananas in the world's shops are clones of a few kinds. Three people give their views.

views.who: A farmer who grows bananas for sale
views.says: Clones are reliable. Every plant gives the same fruit, the same size, the same taste, and buyers know what they will get.
Clones are risky. If a disease arrives that can harm one plant, it can harm every plant. We have seen it happen before.
We should keep many different kinds of banana, including wild ones with seeds, so that we have something to use if a disease comes.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Give a reason from what you know about clones and seeds. Then say what another person gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses the idea that clones are copies and so share the same weaknesses, and seeds give variety. The farmer is right that clones are reliable and convenient. The disease scientist and the seed bank scientist are right that variety is a kind of insurance. A strong answer may suggest keeping many kinds, as the seed bank scientist says.
items.why: Clones are convenient, but a field of identical plants can be wiped out by one disease. Keeping variety is a kind of insurance.

items.p: A log has six rings that match a living tree's rings from 1985 to 1990. The newest ring on the log was formed in the year ____.
items.why: The oldest ring of the log matches 1985 and the newest matches 1990. So the log was cut in 1990 or soon after. Scientists match patterns like this to date old beams.

items.p: A banana stem that has made its bunch of bananas goes on living for many more years.
items.why: False. A banana stem flowers once, makes a single bunch and then dies. The clump goes on because new stems grow from suckers at the base.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Potato, ginger, onion, bhindi.
items.why: Potato, ginger and onion are storage parts of plants: a swollen stem, a rhizome and a bulb. A bhindi is a fruit, with seeds inside, that grows from a flower.

items.p: Match each plant to the sign that tells them when to flower.
pairs: nights getting longer after the monsoon
reaching a big enough size, whatever the day length
items.why: Plants use different signs. Traditional rice measures the night, apple trees remember the winter, coriander responds to long days, and tomatoes are day-neutral and flower when they are big enough.

items.p: Why do many scientists think a plant that lives a long time, like a mango tree, grows slowly, while a plant that lives a short time, like a moong plant, grows quickly?
opts: Each plant spends energy in a different way: on growing and surviving, or on seeds quickly
Mango trees do not use sunlight
Slow growth always means a short life
items.why: A plant has only so much energy. A moong plant puts it into growing fast and making seeds quickly. A mango tree puts it into thick wood, deep roots and surviving for many years of fruiting. Neither is better. They are different ways to spend a life.

items.p: Draw a timeline for a moong plant, a papaya plant and a mango tree. Use one centimetre for each year and mark how long each lives. Show what you notice about the moong plant.
items.a: A line with marks at 0.25 centimetres for a moong plant, about 4 centimetres for a papaya plant and about 100 centimetres for a mango tree. The moong plant is a tiny speck.
items.why: A scale shows how small the moong plant's lifespan is next to a tree's. At one centimetre for a year, 3 months is a quarter of a centimetre.
