items.art: An empty line with a 0 mark at the left end.

items.p: A neighbour keeps her coriander in a closed box in the fruit bowl next to ripe bananas and complains that the leaves go yellow in two days. Give her advice, and give two reasons from what you know.
items.a: Move the coriander away from the bananas, because ripe bananas give off ethylene, which pushes leaves to age. Keep the stems in a little water, or wrap the leaves in a damp cloth, so the leaves do not dry out. Keep them cool, and let air reach the leaves, because a sealed box can make leaves slimy.
items.why: A strong answer names the ripe bananas and ethylene as a cause of yellowing, and gives a plan for cool, damp and airy storage.

items.p: Pando is a grove of more than 40,000 quaking aspen trunks in Utah that all grow from one root system. Why is it hard to say how old Pando is?
opts: The trunks are young, but the root system could be much older, and nobody can count its age directly
Pando is too big to measure
items.why: Each trunk lives only a few decades, but the shared root system goes on and can produce new trunks. Counting rings gives the age of one trunk, not of the whole clone. Scientists have only estimates, and they disagree.

items.p: A fern needs a film of water for its sperm to swim to its egg.
items.why: True. The sperm of a fern swim through a thin film of water to the egg, which is why ferns live in damp places.

items.p: A plant that waits for many years and then flowers once and dies has put almost all it has into that one flowering.
items.why: True. A plant like a talipot palm or an agave stores up energy for years, and spends it on a huge flowering. After that, nothing is left, and the plant dies.

experiments.title: Ripe in a Bag: does a ripe banana ripen a raw mango?
experiments.context: This is the ripening bag test. You put hard green mangoes in three places: in a bag with a ripe banana, in a bag alone and in the open. Then you check each day to see which one ripens first.
experiments.question: Does a ripe banana make a hard green mango ripen sooner, even if the two never touch?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After four days, which mango will be softest: the one in a bag with a ripe banana, the one in a bag alone, or the one left in the open? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The three mangoes are the same kind, the same size and equally hard. They sit in the same warm room, out of the sun. Both bags are the same kind of paper bag, folded shut the same way. Compare A with B to see the banana. Compare B with C to see the bag. You check at the same time every day, and press with the same thumb.
results_table: A: mango with a ripe banana in a bag (colour and softness 1 to 5)
B: mango alone in a bag

materials.item: 3 hard green mangoes of the same kind and size. Mangoes are in the shops mostly from March to July. Out of season, or if they cost too much, use 3 green bananas from one hand (the clearest and cheapest choice, with a result in 2 to 4 days) or 3 hard green tomatoes.
1 very ripe banana with many brown spots. A very ripe one gives off the most gas.
2 brown paper bags, or two bags made from newspaper
a plate to hold fruit C
a pencil, paper, and labels for A, B and C

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts and checks the mangoes at the end. Wash the mangoes before eating. Mango sap near the stalk can sting the skin and lips, so wash your hands. Do not give mango to anyone who is allergic to it. Do not eat any fruit that smells sour or fizzy, or looks rotten. Keep the banana and mangoes out of reach of pets.

schedule.what: Guess. Put mango A with the banana in a bag, mango B in a bag alone and mango C on a plate. Fold the bags shut.
Open the bags for a minute. Press each mango and write the colour and softness.
Check again.
Check again.
Check again.
Check for the last time. A grown-up cuts the mangoes. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Use the softness scale: 1 is hard as a stone, 2 is firm, 3 gives a little, 4 is soft, 5 is very soft. Draw the three mangoes on the last day, with their colours. Draw a bar chart of the softness on day 4. Also write the first day each fruit showed yellow and the first day it reached 3 (gives a little). The day it first changes is a better measure than the final softness.

setup.art: A hard green mango and a spotty ripe banana lying together inside an open brown paper bag labelled A.
setup.caption: 1. Put mango A and the ripe banana in bag A.

setup.art: A second mango alone in a bag labelled B, and a third mango alone on a plate labelled C, all on a kitchen shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Put mango B in bag B. Put mango C on a plate. Fold the bags shut.

setup.art: A child opening a bag for a minute, pressing a mango with a thumb and writing in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, open the bags, press the mangoes and write down what you find.

setup.art: Three mangoes side by side on a plate, one yellow, one half yellow and one still green, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 4. On the last day, line up the three mangoes and compare them.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: softness of the mangoes on day 4 (1 is hard, 5 is very soft)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different, and the gaps can be small.

flow.context: This is the first step of the ripening bag test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the mangoes, the banana and the bags. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: We will put a hard green mango with a ripe banana in a bag. Another mango goes in a bag alone. A third sits in the open. Which will be softest after four days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three mangoes. One has a banana. Which ripens first? Why?

ask.q: Why might the mango with the banana ripen first, or not?
good: The banana is ripe and gives it something.
The banana is sweet and warms the mango.
The bag keeps the smell in.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guess at the top of the table. Choose the hardest green mangoes you can find. Mangoes that are already turning yellow will not show a clear difference. Who: one child does everything and a parent presses a second time to check. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one fruit (A, B or C), presses it and says the number out loud, and a different child writes it down. Swap jobs each day. If you have more children than fruit, each pair can run its own A, B and C with cheap green bananas.

flow.context: In this step you set up the three mangoes.
flow.do: 1. Put mango A and the ripe banana into bag A. 2. Put mango B alone into bag B. 3. Put mango C on a plate. 4. Fold the top of each bag over twice. 5. Label all three. 6. Put all three side by side on a shelf, out of the sun.
flow.say: The banana and mango A share a bag. They do not touch the other mangoes. Fold the bags loosely, not tightly. Put all three in the same warm place.
flow.kid: Put mango A and the banana in bag A. Mango B goes in bag B. Mango C goes on a plate.
flow.parent: Use paper bags, not plastic. Plastic holds in water and can make fruit rot. Keep all three together in a warm place, about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius if you can. If the room is cool (below about 20 degrees in winter), ripening is slow, so put the fruit on a warm shelf and wait longer. In damp monsoon weather paper bags go soft and fruit can grow white fuzz. Use dry bags, swap a wet bag for a fresh one, and write down that you did.

check.q: Why is mango B in a bag alone?
options: To show if the bag alone makes a difference
So the banana is not lonely
So that B is hidden
check.why: If only A had a bag, we would not know if the banana or the bag did the work. B is in a bag with no banana. Comparing A with B shows the banana. Comparing B with C shows the bag.

flow.context: In this step you check the mangoes each day for four days.
flow.do: Each day: 1. Open each bag for a minute. 2. Press each mango gently with your thumb. 3. Look at the colour. 4. Smell it. 5. Write down the colour and the softness. 6. Fold the bags shut again.
flow.say: Check the mangoes at the same time each day. Press gently with your thumb. How soft is each one? Has the colour changed? Does it smell sweet yet?
flow.kid: Open the bags. Press each mango gently. Write down what you find.
flow.parent: On the first day or two, you will probably see little change. By day 3 or 4 mango A is often a little softer and yellower. The gap may be one or two days. If all three look the same, write that down. It can mean the mangoes were already ripening, or the room was cool. If all three still look the same on day 6, do not give up: carry on checking until day 8. A hard, sour raw mango can need a week or more to soften, and that is why green bananas or a mango with a yellow tinge at the stalk work better. A flat result is still a result: write it down and say what you would change.
flow.wait: Check each day for four days, about 3 minutes

flow.context: In this step you compare the three mangoes on the last day.
flow.do: 1. On day 6, check all three mangoes for the last time. 2. Line them up. 3. Draw them. 4. A grown-up cuts each one open and compares the flesh. 5. Draw a bar chart of the softness on day 4.
flow.say: Look at the three mangoes side by side. Which is softest? Which is yellowest? Which is still hard? Is that what you guessed?
flow.kid: Line up the mangoes. Which is softest? A grown-up cuts them open.

ask.q: The banana never touched the mango. How could it change the mango?
good: Something goes from the banana to the mango.
A smell or a gas.
The bag keeps the banana's air close to the mango.

flow.parent: Let your child say how the banana could change the mango before you explain. If the mango with the banana ripened first, the gas is called ethylene. The banana makes it, and the mango can sense it. The bag keeps the gas from drifting away.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think a ripe banana does to a raw mango? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a ripe banana makes a mango ripen sooner. What I saw: on day 4 the mango with the banana was soft and yellow. The one in the bag alone was firm, and the one in the open was hardest. Why: the banana gave off a gas, which the bag kept close. The gas tells raw fruit to ripen. The gas is called ethylene. Your results may differ. If the gaps were small, say that, and say what you would change.
flow.think: If a ripe fruit can change a raw fruit through the air, what do you think a ripe fruit does to the fruit hanging on the same tree?

experiments.title: What Makes a Leaf Give Up Its Green? Darkness, or a ripe banana?
experiments.context: This is a leaf ageing test. You put palak or coriander leaves in three places: in the light, in the dark, and in the dark with a ripe banana. Then you watch which leaves yellow first.
experiments.question: Do leaves turn yellow faster in the dark? Does a ripe banana nearby make them turn yellow faster still?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. By day 6, which leaves will be yellowest: the ones in the light, the ones in the dark, or the ones in the dark with a ripe banana? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three bunches have the same kind of leaves, the same number of leaves, the same size glass and the same water. Both boxes are the same kind of box with a loose lid. Compare the dark box with the light shelf to see the effect of darkness. Compare the two dark boxes to see the effect of the banana.
results_table: B: dark box with a ripe banana
C: dark box with no banana

materials.item: 15 fresh palak leaves, or a bunch of coriander, split into three equal bunches. Choose leaves of the same age and size, with no yellow patches. Coriander sprigs with stems work well.
3 glasses, each with 2 centimetres of water

2 boxes with loose lids, each big enough to hold a glass (and, in one of them, a banana): cardboard boxes, large steel dabbas, or a deep pot with a plate on top. The lid must shut out the light but must not be taped airtight.
1 very ripe banana
a colour scale: with green and yellow crayons or pencils, draw 5 patches from fresh green to yellow, numbered 1 to 5
a pencil, paper and labels

experiments.safety: Do not eat the leaves from this test. Throw away any leaves that smell bad. Wash your hands afterwards. Keep the lids on, because a ripe banana in a box can attract fruit flies. Do not tape the boxes airtight.

schedule.what: Guess. Make three bunches. Put bunch A on a bright shelf, bunch B with the banana in a dark box and bunch C in a dark box alone.
Take a quick look at all three and write the colours.
Look again.
Look again.
Look at the leaves for the last time. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with the colour of each bunch on each day, using the colour scale. Draw one leaf from each bunch on the last day, coloured as you see it.

setup.art: Three glasses of water, each with five palak leaves standing in them, labelled A, B and C, beside a drawn colour scale from green to yellow.
setup.caption: 1. Put five leaves in water in each of three glasses. Label them A, B and C.

setup.art: Glass A on a bright shelf, glass B inside a closed box with a ripe banana, and glass C inside a second closed box alone.
setup.caption: 2. Put A on a bright shelf. Put B in a box with the banana. Put C in a box alone.

setup.art: A child opening a box lid in a dim room to look at the leaves, and matching a leaf to a colour scale.
setup.caption: 3. On days 3, 4 and 5, take a quick look. Match each bunch to the colour scale.

setup.art: Three leaves side by side, one green, one half yellow and one fully yellow, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 4. On day 6, compare one leaf from each bunch.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: yellowness of the leaves on day 5 (1 is fresh green, 5 is yellow)

data.label: B: dark box with a banana

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the leaf ageing test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the leaves, the boxes and the banana. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: We have three bunches of leaves. One stays in the light. One goes in a dark box. One goes in a dark box with a ripe banana. Which will turn yellow first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three bunches of leaves. Which turns yellow first? Why?

ask.q: Why might leaves turn yellow in the dark?
good: They cannot make food in the dark.
The leaf gives up when it is useless.
The dark makes them sad.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.context: In this step you set up the three bunches.
flow.do: 1. Make three bunches of five leaves. 2. Stand each bunch in a glass with 2 centimetres of water. 3. Put bunch A on a bright shelf. 4. Put bunch B in a box with a ripe banana beside it. 5. Put bunch C in a second box alone. 6. Put on the lids.
flow.say: Each box has a lid, but not a tight one. The banana sits beside the leaves, and does not touch them. Check that everything is the same, except for the banana and the light.
flow.kid: Make three bunches. Put one in the light. Put one in a box with a banana. Put one in a box alone.
flow.parent: Keep all three bunches in the same warm room. Keep the water at the same level. Use fresh leaves with no yellow patches. Who: one child does all three. With 2 to 4 children, each child looks after one bunch (and a fourth child can score all three). For a fair score, the child who did not set up a bunch gives its colour number. Look at the leaves at the same time each day, in the same light, with the colour scale held next to the leaf.

check.q: Why does box C have leaves but no banana?
options: So we can tell the effect of the dark from the effect of the banana
So the leaves are not lonely
To keep the banana safe
check.why: Box B has dark and a banana. Box C has dark only. If B yellows faster than C, the banana made the difference. If C yellows faster than A, the dark made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you check the leaves each day for three days.
flow.do: Each day for days 3, 4 and 5: 1. Open each box for less than a minute. 2. Match each bunch to the colour scale. 3. Smell the leaves. 4. Write down the numbers. 5. Close the boxes.
flow.say: Quickly now. What colour is each bunch? Match each one to your scale. Which is the yellowest?
flow.kid: Take a quick look. Match each bunch to the colour scale. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Palak and coriander often start to yellow after about three to five days in the dark, but this depends on the warmth. Cut leaves in water may also go limp or slimy before they turn yellow, especially in hot, humid weather. Score a slimy leaf as 5 and write 'slimy' in the notes. If all three still look the same on day 6, keep looking until day 8. If they still look the same, write that down: it is a real result.
flow.wait: Check on days 3, 4 and 5, about 3 minutes each

flow.context: In this step you compare the three leaves on the last day.
flow.do: On day 6, take a leaf from each bunch and lay them side by side. Match each to the colour scale. Draw them. Draw a bar chart of the colour numbers.
flow.say: Look at the three leaves. Which is greenest? Which is yellowest? What do you think happened to the green?
flow.kid: Lay one leaf from each bunch side by side. Which is yellowest?

ask.q: What do you think happened to the green in the yellow leaves?
good: It was taken apart.
The leaf stopped making green.
The plant took the useful parts back.

flow.parent: The green is chlorophyll. When a leaf ageing programme starts, the plant takes the chlorophyll apart and moves out the nitrogen. The yellow was in the leaf all along and shows once the green goes. A leaf cut from the plant cannot send the nitrogen anywhere, but the programme still starts.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think makes a leaf turn yellow? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: darkness and a ripe banana both make leaves turn yellow sooner. What I saw: the leaves in the light stayed green. The dark leaves went pale. The dark leaves with the banana went yellow first. Why: in the dark a leaf cannot make food, so the plant takes the leaf apart. Ethylene from the banana speeds that up. If your result is different, say so.
flow.think: Why might it be wise to store palak and coriander away from ripe bananas?

experiments.title: Node or No Node? Where does a money plant grow new roots?
experiments.context: This is a cutting test. You cut a money plant vine into three kinds of piece and see which ones grow roots in water. You find out where the roots come from, and whether a leaf helps.
experiments.question: Where on a money plant stem do new roots grow? Does a leaf help the roots grow?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cuttings will grow roots: the ones with a node and a leaf, the ones with a node and no leaf, or the ones with no node? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All nine cuttings come from the same vine and are about the same length (cuttings A and B are about 8 centimetres; C is as long as the gap between two nodes allows, at least 4 centimetres, and you write its length down). All three jars have the same water, in the same bright place, out of hot sun. Only one thing differs between the jars: the node and the leaf.
results_table: Jar A: node and leaf (roots, length in mm)

materials.item: a healthy money plant vine about 60 centimetres long with at least 8 leaves, or two shorter vines. Most families trim their plant often, so ask a neighbour for cuttings.
a pair of scissors for a grown-up
3 clear jars or bottles, each holding 3 cuttings, filled with 5 centimetres of water
a ruler, a marker and labels for A, B and C
a magnifying glass, if you have one. A phone camera zoomed in works as well.

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with scissors. Money plant sap can irritate skin and is harmful if eaten, so wash your hands after touching the cut stems. Keep the jars away from pets and small children.

schedule.what: Guess. A grown-up cuts nine pieces. Set up three jars.
Look for roots and write what you see.
Look again.
Look again.
Measure the roots. Draw the jars. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on each day. Draw one cutting from each jar on day 15 and mark where the roots are. Write the length in millimetres of the longest root on each cutting.

setup.art: A money plant vine laid on a table with three kinds of piece marked: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node and no leaf, and one with no node.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts nine pieces: three with a node and a leaf, three with a node and no leaf, and three with no node.

setup.art: Three jars of water, each with three cuttings leaning in them, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 2. Put the cuttings in the jars. Put the node under the water.

setup.art: A child looking at the node of a cutting in a jar through a magnifying glass, with white root tips showing.
setup.caption: 3. Look for roots every few days. Measure them with a ruler.

setup.art: Three cuttings side by side on a plate, one with many long roots, one with a few short roots and one with none.
setup.caption: 4. On day 15, compare the roots.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: length of the longest root on day 15 (millimetres)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up to show a possible pattern. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the cutting test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the vine. Point to a node, a small bump on the stem where a leaf joins, and to the small brown root stubs there. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it in the table.
flow.say: A node is a bump on the stem where a leaf joins. We will cut the vine into pieces and put them in water. Which will grow roots? Where will they come from? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find a node on the vine. Which cuttings will grow roots? Why?

ask.q: Where on the stem do you think the roots will come from?
good: From the node, where the leaf joins.
From the cut end.
From anywhere on the stem.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Note that a money plant already has small aerial roots at the nodes. That is a clue your child might notice.

flow.context: In this step an adult cuts nine pieces from the vine.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts nine pieces from the vine. 2. Cut three pieces that each have a node and one leaf. 3. Cut three that have a node, and take the leaf off at the stalk. 4. Cut three plain pieces between two nodes, with no node and no leaf. 5. Keep pieces A and B about 8 centimetres long, with the node near the bottom. Cut piece C from the stretch between two nodes, as long as the gap allows (at least 4 centimetres), and write down its length.
flow.say: Each piece is about the same length. Some have a node and a leaf. Some have a node and no leaf. Some have no node at all. The piece with no node is the one to watch.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts nine pieces. Make three of each kind. Keep them in groups.
flow.parent: Cut cleanly with sharp scissors. Money plant stems are often short between nodes, so a plain piece may be shorter than the others. That is fine, as long as you write its length down and keep it under the water. Look for the stretch of stem with no bump and no leaf stalk.

flow.context: In this step you set up the three jars.
flow.do: 1. Put three cuttings into each jar. 2. Put jar A as the node-and-leaf group, jar B as the node-and-no-leaf group and jar C as the no-node group. 3. Check that the node is under the water in A and B. 4. Label the jars. 5. Put them in a bright place out of hot sun.
flow.say: Each jar holds one kind of cutting. The nodes in jars A and B go under the water. Put the jars in a bright place, but out of hot sun.
flow.kid: Put three cuttings in each jar. Nodes go under the water. Label the jars.
flow.parent: Change the water every three days, or top it up if it falls. Keep the water clean. A slimy jar should be washed and refilled. Who: one child sets up all three jars. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns a jar and measures its roots, and a different child writes the numbers down. Or each child can set up a full set of nine cuttings for a bigger sample.

check.q: Why do we use three cuttings of each kind and not just one?
options: One cutting might fail by chance, and three give a fairer answer
Three jars look better
To use up the vine
check.why: A single cutting might die for a reason that has nothing to do with the test. With three, one odd result matters much less.

flow.context: In this step you check for roots on days 5, 8 and 11.
flow.do: On days 5, 8 and 11: 1. Look at each cutting. 2. Look for white root tips, using the magnifying glass. 3. Measure any roots with a ruler. 4. Write what you find. 5. Top up the water.
flow.say: Look closely at each node. Do you see any white tips? How long are they? Write down what you find.
flow.kid: Look at the cuttings. Find any roots. Measure them. Write them down.
flow.parent: Roots often appear at the nodes in about one to two weeks, and more slowly in cool winter weather, when it may take three weeks. Cuttings with a leaf are often a little quicker. The cuttings with no node usually grow nothing and may go soft at the cut. If nothing has rooted by day 11, give it up to ten more days and keep topping up the water.
flow.wait: Check on days 5, 8 and 11, about 3 minutes each

flow.context: In this step you measure the roots on the last day.
flow.do: On day 15, take out the cuttings from each jar. Measure the longest root on each. Write down the numbers. Draw one cutting from each jar and mark where the roots came from.
flow.say: Look at the cuttings. Where did the roots come from? Which jar has the longest roots? Which has none?
flow.kid: Measure the roots on each cutting. Draw one from each jar.

ask.q: Where did the roots grow?
good: At the nodes.
Not from the plain stem.
More roots came from the cutting with a leaf.

flow.parent: Roots grow from the nodes, where the plant keeps cells that can become roots. A leaf makes food and a growth hormone called auxin, which flows to the cut end and helps roots start. So the cuttings with a leaf usually grow more roots, sooner.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about where roots grow? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: roots grow from nodes, and a leaf helps. What I saw: the cuttings with a node and a leaf grew the longest roots, the ones with a node and no leaf grew a few short roots, and the plain pieces grew none. Why: the node holds the cells that can turn into roots, and the leaf supplies food and a growth message. Each rooted cutting is a clone of the vine. If the leafless cuttings rooted as well as the leaf ones, say so. That is a real finding and the explanation about the leaf may be only part of the story.
flow.think: All three cuttings in jar A came from the same vine. Are they the same plant, or three plants?

experiments.title: Shelf, Window or Fridge? Where does a green tomato ripen?
experiments.context: This is a ripening place test. You put hard green tomatoes in three places: on a warm shelf, on a bright windowsill and in the fridge. Then you find out where they ripen best.
experiments.question: Does a hard green tomato ripen best on a warm shelf, in a bright window or in the fridge? What happens to the fridge tomato when it comes out?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After six days, which tomato will be reddest, and which will be greenest? Why do you think so? What will happen to the fridge tomato if you take it out?
experiments.fair_test: All three tomatoes are the same kind, the same size and equally green. Each one sits in a paper bag, folded shut the same way. Only the place is different. You check at the same time each day.
results_table: Warm shelf: colour 1 to 5 (1 is green, 5 is red)

materials.item: 3 hard green tomatoes of the same kind and size, from one pile. Pick pale or whitish green ones, not dark green: very dark green tomatoes may shrivel before they ripen. Better and cheaper: 3 green bananas from one hand. They turn yellow in a few days, and the one from the fridge turns grey-brown. Hard green mangoes can do instead.
3 brown paper bags
a room thermometer or a phone that can show the temperature, if you have one. If you have none, write warm, cool or cold from how the place feels.
labels, a pencil and paper, and crayons for a colour scale from 1 (green) to 5 (red)

experiments.safety: Do not eat a tomato that smells sour or looks rotten. Wash your hands after touching the tomatoes. Write 'science, do not eat' on the fridge bag, so nobody cooks it by mistake.

schedule.what: Guess. Put one tomato in a bag on a warm shelf, one in a bag on a bright windowsill and one in a bag in the fridge.
Check the colour and softness.
Check again.
Take the fridge tomato out and put it on the warm shelf. Compare.
Check again.
Check for the last time. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each time you check. Write the temperature of each place if you can. Draw the three tomatoes on day 6 and again on day 12.

setup.art: Three hard green tomatoes, each in a folded brown paper bag, labelled Shelf, Window and Fridge.
setup.caption: 1. Put each green tomato in its own paper bag. Label the bags.

setup.art: One bag on a warm kitchen shelf, one on a bright windowsill and one on a shelf inside a fridge.
setup.caption: 2. Put one bag in each place.

setup.art: A child holding up three tomatoes, one red, one orange and one still green.
setup.caption: 3. Every two days, open the bags and compare the colours.

setup.art: The fridge tomato placed on the warm shelf next to a note that says Day 6.
setup.caption: 4. On day 6, move the fridge tomato to the warm shelf.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: colour of each tomato over time (1 is green, 5 is red)
example_chart.note: This line shows the warm shelf tomato in a made-up example. The fridge tomato would stay near 1 until it comes out.

flow.context: This is the first step of the ripening place test. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the tomatoes and the three places. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it in the table.
flow.say: We will put three green tomatoes in three places. One goes on a warm shelf. One goes on a window. One goes in the fridge. Which will be red first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three tomatoes, three places. Which ripens first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the fridge tomato will ripen slowly, or not at all?
good: It is too cold for it to change.
Cold stops things from working.
A fridge is dark.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the window will be best because of the sun. Write down their reason. Who: one child does everything. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one place and one bag. All the children guess first, then each one checks and scores their own bag. The writer rotates.

flow.context: In this step you put the three tomatoes in their three places.
flow.do: 1. Put each tomato in its own paper bag. 2. Fold each bag shut. 3. Put one on the warm shelf, one in the bright window and one in the fridge. 4. Label the bags. 5. Write the temperature of each place, if you can.
flow.say: Each tomato gets a bag. The bags are all the same. Only the place is different. Put one on the shelf, one in the window and one in the fridge.
flow.kid: Put each tomato in a bag. Put one on the shelf, one in the window and one in the fridge.
flow.parent: The window should be bright but not in hot sun for hours, which can bake the tomato. The fridge should be a normal one, not the freezer.

check.q: Why does each tomato sit in a paper bag of the same kind?
options: So only the place is different
So the tomatoes cannot see out
So the bags get used
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one tomato had no bag, we would not know if the place or the bag made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you check the tomatoes on days 3 and 5.
flow.do: On days 3 and 5 (and again on day 9): 1. Open each bag for a minute. 2. Match each tomato to the colour scale. 3. Press it gently. 4. Write down the colour and the softness. 5. Fold the bags shut.
flow.say: Open each bag. What colour is each tomato? Is it soft? Write it down.
flow.kid: Check each tomato. Write its colour. Press it gently.
flow.parent: In a warm room (25 to 30 degrees) a mature green tomato typically starts to turn pink in about four to eight days. Slower in a cool room. The window tomato may be a little quicker or slower, depending on the warmth. The fridge tomato usually stays green and firm. Do not promise a red tomato by day 6. If nothing has changed on any tomato, wait: the later checks will show it.
flow.wait: Check on days 3 and 5, about 3 minutes each

flow.context: In this step you move the fridge tomato to the warm shelf and compare all three.
flow.do: On day 6: 1. Take the fridge tomato out of the fridge. 2. Put it on the warm shelf, in its bag. 3. Compare all three tomatoes. 4. Draw them.
flow.say: The fridge tomato has been cold for six days. Let's warm it up. Will it ripen now? Will it ripen as well as the others?
flow.kid: Take the fridge tomato out. Put it on the warm shelf. Compare all three.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the fridge tomato now?
good: It will start to ripen slowly.
It will ripen as well as the others.
It might go soft and pale without turning red.

flow.parent: A tomato that has been cold for days often ripens slowly and patchy after warming, and may stay pale or go mealy. Cold can damage fruit from warm places. That is why ripening fruit is best kept out of the fridge.

flow.context: In this step you check the tomatoes on the last day.
flow.do: On day 12, check all three tomatoes for the last time. Match each to the colour scale. Write down your results. Cut the tomatoes open and look at the flesh.
flow.say: Look at all three tomatoes. Which is reddest? Which is softest? How does the fridge tomato look inside?
flow.kid: Check all three tomatoes. Which is reddest? Cut one open.
flow.parent: Let a grown-up cut the tomatoes. Look at the colour and the feel of the flesh. A tomato damaged by cold can look watery or mealy inside.

flow.context: In this step you say what the test showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about where fruit ripen best? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: fruit ripen best in a warm place and not in the fridge. What I saw: the shelf tomato turned pink first, the window tomato was a little behind or ahead, and the fridge tomato stayed green. After warming, it ripened slowly or in patches. Your days and colours will differ. Why: ripening is chemistry, and chemistry runs slowly in the cold. A long spell in the cold can also damage a fruit from a warm place. A ripe fruit can go in the fridge to slow it down.
flow.think: If you want to keep a ripe mango for another day, where would you put it?

activities.title: The Sleeping Pantry: which kitchen foods are a plant's savings?
activities.context: In this activity, you set up carrot, beetroot, onion, potato, sweet potato and ginger on saucers of water. You find out which of them can grow shoots using the food they carry.

materials.item: the cut top of a carrot and of a beetroot, about 3 centimetres thick, with a bit of the stalk
an onion, a potato that already shows eyes or tiny sprouts, a sweet potato and a piece of ginger with a bump on it
saucers, shallow bowls or jar lids, and water
toothpicks, a marker, labels and a ruler
a knife, for a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the tops and pushes in the toothpicks, which are sharp. Do not eat potatoes that have turned green or sprouted, because they can make you ill. Do not eat any of the foods from this activity after they have sat in water for days. If a food smells bad or grows fuzzy mould, throw it away, wash the saucer and write 'rotted' in the table. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess. A grown-up cuts the tops. Set out all six foods.
Look at the foods and measure any shoots.
Look again.
Measure the shoots. Draw them. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.record: A table with six foods. For each one, write your guess, the day a shoot or root first showed, and the longest shoot on day 10. Draw the three that grew the most.

setup.art: A carrot top and a beetroot top, cut side down, in saucers with 1 centimetre of water.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the tops off a carrot and a beetroot. Stand them cut side down in a saucer of water.

setup.art: An onion with the bottom in a small jar of water held up by toothpicks, and a potato and a sweet potato half in water.
setup.caption: 2. Hold an onion, a sweet potato and a potato on the rim of a jar, with the bottom in water.

setup.art: A piece of ginger on a damp cloth on a saucer, next to the others on a bright shelf.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the ginger on a damp cloth. Put all six on a bright shelf.

setup.art: A child measuring a feathery green carrot shoot with a ruler and writing in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Look every few days. Measure the shoots.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sleeping Pantry. You guess before you start.
flow.do: Show your child the six foods. Ask which parts of the plant they are and which ones will sprout. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Each of these foods is a store of food. A plant saved it for later. Which ones do you think will grow green shoots? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six foods from the kitchen. Which will grow shoots? Why?

ask.q: Which part of a plant do you think a carrot is, a root, a stem or a leaf?
good: A root.
A stem.
I am not sure.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A carrot and a beetroot are swollen roots. An onion is a bulb, made of thick leaf bases on a tiny stem. A potato is a swollen underground stem. A sweet potato is a swollen root, and ginger is a rhizome, a thick underground stem. Who: one child sets out all six. With 2 to 4 children, each child takes two or three foods and guesses for them, then they compare. The cost is small: all six foods are a few rupees at a kirana.

flow.context: In this step you set out the six foods.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a 3 centimetre top from the carrot and the beetroot. 2. Stand each cut side down in a saucer with 1 centimetre of water. 3. Push toothpicks into the sides of the onion, the potato and the sweet potato. Rest each on the rim of a jar of water, with the bottom just in the water. 4. Lay the ginger on a damp cloth on a saucer. 5. Label them and put them on a bright shelf.
flow.say: Each food sits in or on water. We are giving each of them water and warmth, and nothing else. No soil and no fertiliser.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the tops. Put each food on water. Label them all.
flow.parent: Change the water every two days, or top it up. Some potatoes, onions and ginger from shops are treated to stop them from sprouting, and a fresh potato may be asleep for weeks. That is why we choose a potato with eyes. Ginger is slow and may need two to four weeks, so do not be surprised if it does nothing in ten days. Carrot and beetroot tops that were cut off at the shop may sprout only weakly. If a food does not sprout, that is a result too. Write it down, and try another one if you wish.

check.q: These foods have no soil and no fertiliser. Where will a shoot get its food?
options: From the food stored inside the carrot, onion or potato
From the water alone
From the saucer
check.why: The stored food in the swollen root, stem or bulb feeds the new shoot, just as the food in a seed feeds the baby plant. Water alone has no food.

flow.context: In this step you check the foods on days 4 and 7.
flow.do: On days 4 and 7: 1. Look at each food. 2. Measure any roots or shoots. 3. Write down what you find. 4. Top up the water.
flow.say: Has anything changed? Look for white roots and green shoots. Measure them. Which one is growing fastest?
flow.kid: Look at each food. Measure any shoots. Write down what you find.
flow.parent: Onion usually grows roots in two or three days, and a green shoot soon after. Carrot and beetroot tops make leaves in a week. Sweet potato makes leafy shoots in one to two weeks.
flow.wait: Check on days 4 and 7, about 3 minutes each

flow.context: In this step you measure and draw the shoots on the last day.
flow.do: On day 10: 1. Measure the longest shoot on each food. 2. Draw the three that grew the most. 3. Sort the foods into those that grew shoots and those that did not.
flow.say: Which foods grew shoots? How long are they? Are the shoots green? How do they get their food?
flow.kid: Measure the longest shoot on each food. Draw the three best.

ask.q: The carrot top grew leaves. Will the carrot top grow a new carrot?
good: No, the top will just grow leaves.
It has no new root to store food.
The leaves live on the old carrot.

flow.parent: The leaves are using the food stored in the carrot top. They cannot make a new carrot, because a carrot is a store, not a seed. The foods that did not sprout may have been treated, or been too old. Write that down.

flow.context: In this step you say what the activity showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think these foods are for? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a carrot, an onion and a potato are food stores for the plant. What I saw: the shoots grew with just water, using the stored food. Why: in the good season the plant made more food than the plant needed, and saved it so it could restart in the next season. A carrot plant, left alone, spends the savings in the second year to flower and make seeds.
flow.think: We eat these stores. What would a carrot plant do if we did not?

activities.title: Spore Print: the dust under a fern leaf
activities.context: In this activity, you make a print from the brown dots under a fern leaf. You see the dust that ferns use instead of seeds, and meet the first step of a fern's life cycle.

materials.item: 1 fern frond with dark brown or black dots on the underside. Roadside and garden ferns often have them in the rainy season and after. Many pot ferns in flats have none yet. Ask the owner first.
2 sheets of white paper
a bowl or glass to cover the frond
a magnifying glass, if you have one. A phone camera zoomed in works as well.
a clear tub with a lid and some damp soil, if you want to try growing the spores

activities.safety: Ask the owner before you cut a frond. Do not blow on the spores or breathe them in. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess. Find a frond with brown dots. Lay it dots-down on white paper under a bowl.
Lift the frond. Look at the print and the dots.

activities.record: Draw the underside of the frond with its rows of dots, and the print the frond left on the paper. Write what the dust looks like.

setup.art: The underside of a fern frond showing neat rows of brown dots.
setup.caption: 1. Turn a fern frond over and find the rows of brown dots.

setup.art: A fern frond lying dots-down on white paper with a bowl turned over it.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the frond dots-down on white paper. Cover it with a bowl.

setup.art: A pale brown dust print in the shape of the frond on white paper, and a child looking at it with a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, lift the frond. Look at the dusty print.

flow.context: This is the first step of Spore Print. You guess before you look.
flow.do: Show your child a fern. Ask what the plant does instead of making flowers and seeds. Write down the guess.
flow.say: A fern never makes flowers or seeds. Yet new ferns appear. How do you think ferns make new ferns? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A fern has no flowers or seeds. How do you think ferns make new ferns?

ask.q: How do you think a fern makes new ferns?
good: Maybe with seeds too small to see.
From pieces of the plant.
From dust under the leaves.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. For hundreds of years, people believed that ferns had invisible seeds. Your child may guess something close to this.

flow.context: In this step you set up the spore print.
flow.do: 1. Find a frond with brown dots on the back. 2. A grown-up cuts it off with scissors. 3. Lay it dots-down on white paper. 4. Cover it with a bowl. 5. Leave it overnight, away from drafts.
flow.say: These brown dots are spore cases. When they are ripe, they let go of a fine dust. We will catch the dust on paper.
flow.kid: Cut a frond with dots on the back. Lay it dots-down on white paper. Cover it with a bowl.
flow.parent: The dots must be dark brown or black to be ripe. Pale green dots are not ripe yet. Not every fern has dots on every frond. Some, such as many ferns in pots, make dots only when they are mature. If you find no dots, try another fern.

flow.context: In this step you look at the print.
flow.do: The next day: 1. Lift the bowl and the frond carefully. 2. Look at the dust on the paper. 3. Look at it with a magnifying glass. 4. Draw it.
flow.say: The paper has a pattern. What do you see? What colour is the dust? Does it look like seeds? Look closely.
flow.kid: Lift the frond. Look at the dust on the paper. Draw what you see.
flow.parent: The dust is a very fine powder, orange-brown or dark brown, in the shape of the frond. It is made of millions of spores. Each is much smaller than a seed. Do not blow on it, and wash your hands. If the paper stays clean after a day, the dots were not ripe. Leave the frond one more day, or try a darker-dotted frond. A pale or tiny print is normal. A print is not guaranteed, so also draw the dots you saw. Who: one frond serves 1 to 4 children, who take turns lifting it and each draw the print. If you find two fronds, two children can each make a print and compare.

check.q: The dust on the paper is a fern's spores. How are spores different from seeds?
options: A spore is a single tiny cell, with no store of food
A spore is a tiny seed
A spore is a tiny flower
check.why: A seed holds a baby plant and a store of food. A spore is a single cell with no food store. The spore must land in a damp place to grow into a tiny plant.

flow.context: In this step you try growing the spores, to see the next stage of the fern life cycle.
flow.do: If you like, sprinkle a little of the dust onto damp soil in a clear tub. Close the lid. Put it in a bright place, not in direct sun. Look every week.
flow.say: A spore that lands on damp soil may grow into a tiny green heart. It may take a month or more. Let's try. Look every week.
flow.kid: Sprinkle some spores on damp soil. Close the lid. Look each week.
flow.parent: This step is optional, and it is not certain to work. If it works, you will see a green film on the soil in three to six weeks. Under a magnifying glass, you may find tiny heart-shaped plants. In these, the sperm swim to the egg through a film of water, which is why ferns need damp places.
flow.think: A fern spore lands on damp soil and grows into a tiny heart-shaped plant. Why do ferns live in damp places?
flow.wait: Look every week for 4 to 8 weeks

activities.title: Read a Tree's Diary: ring widths and dry years
activities.context: In this activity, you read the rings of two trees and find which years were dry. You then match the rings of an old log to a living tree to find out when the log was cut.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a ruler
a cut log, a piece of firewood or a branch slice, if you can find one at a carpenter's or a tree-cutting site

schedule.what: Draw the rings. Find the dry years. Match the log to the tree.

activities.record: Draw the rings of tree A on paper using 5 millimetres of paper for each millimetre of ring, so the widest 6 millimetre ring is a 30 millimetre bar. Mark the narrow rings. Write the years of the two driest years. Write the year the log's last ring was formed.

setup.art: A cut log with rings and a child counting them with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. If you have a real log, count its rings. Look for wide and narrow rings.

setup.art: A paper strip with bars of different widths drawn side by side, labelled with years from 2012 to 2023.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the rings of tree A from the numbers. Each number is a width in millimetres.

setup.art: Three paper strips laid side by side, with the narrow bars lined up.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the strip for the log along tree A until the narrow rings match.

flow.context: This is the first step of Read a Tree's Diary. You look at rings and guess what they mean.
flow.do: If you have a real log or branch, show it. Count the rings and ask what each ring might mean. Otherwise, draw a circle with several rings and ask the same.
flow.say: This is a slice of a tree. Do you see the rings? What do you think each ring means? Why do some rings look wider than others?
flow.kid: Look at the rings. What does each ring mean? Why are some wider?

ask.q: Why might one ring be wider than the next?
good: The tree grew more that year.
There was more rain.
It was a good year.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. In a place with a wet season and a dry season, a tree grows more in the wet season and less in the dry season. One pale and dark pair is usually one year. A wide ring marks a year with good rain.

flow.context: In this step you draw tree A's rings from a list of widths.
flow.do: 1. These are made-up ring widths for practice. Tree A has these ring widths in millimetres, for 2012 to 2023. They are 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 4, 5, 5, 2, 6, 4 and 5. 2. Draw them side by side as bars on a strip of paper, with 5 millimetres of paper for each millimetre of ring. 3. Label each bar with its year. 4. Circle the two narrowest.
flow.say: Each number is the width of one ring. Draw a bar of that width for each year. Label them. Which two years are the narrowest?
flow.kid: Draw tree A's rings from the numbers. Circle the two narrowest rings.
flow.parent: The widths for tree A, from 2012 to 2023, are 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 4, 5, 5, 2, 6, 4 and 5. The two narrowest are 2016 with 1 millimetre and 2020 with 2 millimetres. These were the driest years.

flow.context: In this step you compare a second tree with the first.
flow.do: 1. Tree B was planted in 2016. Its ring widths for 2016 to 2023 are 1, 3, 4, 4, 1, 5, 3, 4. 2. Draw tree B's strip. 3. Compare it with tree A. 4. Which years are narrow in both?
flow.say: Tree B is a different tree in the same place. Does it have narrow rings in the same years as tree A? What does that tell you about those years?
flow.kid: Draw tree B's rings. Are the same years narrow in both trees?
flow.parent: Tree B's ring for 2016 is 1 and for 2020 is 1. They match tree A's two narrow years. This agreement is how scientists tell that the weather was the cause.

check.q: Two trees in the same region both have a narrow ring in the same year. What is the best explanation?
options: The weather that year was poor for all trees, such as a drought
Both trees were chopped
Narrow rings are always made in the same year
check.why: When many trees share a narrow ring in the same year, the cause is shared. A drought is the most likely cause. Scientists use this to read the weather of the past.

flow.context: In this step you match a log's rings to a living tree to find when the log was cut.
flow.do: 1. A log has these ring widths, from its oldest ring to its newest: 1, 4, 5, 5, 2, 6. 2. Draw these on a separate paper strip at the same scale. Slide this strip alongside tree A until the pattern matches. 3. Find the year of the log's newest ring.
flow.say: This log has six rings. The pattern is narrow, medium, wide, wide, narrow, very wide. Can you find where this pattern fits tree A? What year does the last ring belong to?
flow.kid: Slide the log's strip along tree A. Find where the pattern fits.
flow.parent: The pattern 1, 4, 5, 5, 2, 6 matches tree A in the years 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021. So the log's last ring was 2021, and the log was cut in 2021 or soon after. Scientists match old beams in the same way, which is called cross-dating. Who: one child can do everything. With 2 to 4 children, one draws tree A, one draws tree B, one draws the log strip and slides it, and one checks the match. These ring numbers are made up for practice. Real trees in India, especially in the tropics, often show less clear rings.
flow.think: If the log's rings fitted tree A's rings from 2016 to 2021, in what year was the log most likely cut?

activities.safety: Handle a real log with care because it can give splinters. A grown-up at a carpenter's or tree-cutting site does any cutting. Do not saw it yourself.

activities.title: The Lifespan Tape: plants on a very long strip of paper
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a very long strip of paper in which 1 millimetre stands for 1 year. You mark how long different plants live, and see how big the differences are.

materials.item: a long strip of paper 5 metres long: a roll of paper, newspaper sheets taped end to end (about 20 to 25 sheets), or chalk on the floor of a veranda or terrace
a ruler or a tailor's tape, a pencil and a marker. Sticky tape for joining sheets.
a long hallway or a veranda to lay the strip on

schedule.what: Lay out the strip. Mark each plant's lifespan. Compare.

activities.record: Write a table with the plants, their lifespans in years and their length on the tape in millimetres. Photograph or draw the strip.

setup.art: A long strip of paper laid down a hallway with a ruler and a pencil, marked every 100 millimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Tape sheets into a strip. Mark every 100 millimetres, which stands for 100 years.

setup.art: A pencil dot on the strip for a moong plant, and a short line for a papaya plant.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the short lives first: moong, tulsi and papaya.

setup.art: The long strip with marks for a mango, a banyan, a peepal and a bristlecone pine at the far end.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the long lives: mango, banyan, peepal and bristlecone pine.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Lifespan Tape. You guess before you measure.
flow.do: Show your child the list of plants. Ask which will be the longest on the strip and which the shortest. Write the guesses.
flow.say: We will make a strip where one millimetre is one year. How long do you think the strip for a moong plant will be? How long for the oldest tree? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One millimetre is one year. How long will the strip for a moong plant be? For a tree?

ask.q: How long do you think the moong plant's strip will be?
good: A tiny dot.
A few centimetres.
As long as my finger.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children guess far too long for a moong plant. The answer, about 3 months, is a quarter of one millimetre.

flow.context: In this step you measure and mark the plant lifespans on the tape.
flow.do: 1. Tape sheets into a strip about 5 metres long. 2. Mark a 'start' line. 3. Measure and mark each plant: moong 0.25 millimetres, which is a dot. Papaya 4 millimetres. Coconut palm 70 millimetres. Mango tree 100 millimetres. Great Banyan 250 millimetres. Peepal 2,300 millimetres. Bristlecone pine 4,800 millimetres. 4. Write the plant's name at each mark.
flow.say: One millimetre is one year. A moong plant lives about three months. That is a quarter of a millimetre, less than the tip of a pencil. A bristlecone pine is 4,800 millimetres. How long is that?
flow.kid: Make a strip. One millimetre is one year. Mark each plant at the right length.
flow.parent: 4,800 millimetres is 480 centimetres, which is 4 metres and 80 centimetres. The peepal's 2,300 millimetres is 2 metres 30 centimetres. The numbers for the trees are reported and rounded. A coconut palm is given a lifespan of about 70 years, and the Great Banyan is said to be about 250 years old. A moong plant, at about 3 months, is a quarter of a millimetre, which is a speck of a dot. Who: one child can do it alone, but it is faster with 2 to 4: one measures with the tailor's tape, one marks, one writes the names, one checks the numbers. A metre stick or tailor's tape saves a lot of time. For a quick version, use chalk on the floor and skip the taping. All the tree ages here are reported or about, not exact.

check.q: On the tape, a mango tree that lives 100 years is 100 millimetres long. How many centimetres is that?
options: 10 centimetres
100 centimetres
1 centimetre
check.why: 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre. 100 divided by 10 is 10. So the mango's strip is 10 centimetres long.

flow.context: In this step you walk along the strip and compare.
flow.do: Walk along the strip together. Stop at each plant. Ask what surprised your child.
flow.say: Walk along the strip. What is the first mark you can see? Where is the first plant you can see with your eyes? What is the longest? How many moong plants would fit in one year?
flow.kid: Walk along the strip. Which plant is the longest? Which can you hardly see?

ask.q: What surprised you about the strip?
good: The moong is a tiny dot.
The bristlecone pine is so long.
Most plants are very short compared with the pine.

flow.context: In this step you say what the tape showed.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about how long plants live? What did you see on the strip? Why is a plant's lifespan so different from another's?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: plants live for very different lengths of time. What I saw: moong is a dot, a mango is 10 centimetres, and the pine is nearly 5 metres. Why: some plants put their effort into growing fast and making seeds quickly. Others put theirs into growing slowly and surviving for centuries.
flow.think: If a moong plant is a dot and a pine is almost five metres long, can you compare their lives?

activities.safety: Do not leave the strip across a doorway or stairs where someone may trip. Chalk marks wash off with water.

projects.title: Pinch or Let Go: do marigolds flower longer if you pinch the old flowers?
projects.context: In this project, you grow six marigold plants for eight weeks. You pinch off the old flowers on three of them, and let the other three make seeds. You count the flowers to find out which group flowers more.

materials.item: 6 young marigold seedlings of the same size from a nursery
6 pots, old buckets, paint tins or large plastic bottles cut in half, each at least 20 centimetres wide, with holes in the bottom. Reuse what you have to keep the cost low.
potting soil, or garden soil from a park or a neighbour's garden mixed with a little compost or dry manure
a sunny spot with at least 5 hours of direct sun
labels P1, P2, P3 and L1, L2, L3, a pen and a notebook
a bucket or old tub to catch the pinched flowers

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the bottom of each pot or bucket, with a nail or a drill, because these are sharp. Wash your hands after touching soil and marigold plants. Marigold sap can irritate some people's skin, and children who react to chrysanthemum-family plants should wear gloves. Do not let water stand in saucers, because mosquitoes breed in it. Keep the pots away from the edge of a balcony.

schedule.what: Guess. Plant six seedlings in six pots. Label three Pinch and three Let Go.
Count the open flowers on every plant. Pinch the old ones on the Pinch plants.
Count and pinch.
Count and pinch.
Count and pinch.
Count and pinch.
Count and pinch.
Count and pinch.
Count for the last time. Compare the groups. Draw the graph. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

projects.record: A table with six rows, one for each plant, and a column for each week. Write the number of open flowers on each plant at each visit. At the end, add up the flowers for the Pinch group and for the Let Go group, and draw a line graph with a line for each group.

setup.art: Six pots of marigold seedlings in a row on a sunny balcony, labelled P1, P2, P3, L1, L2 and L3.
setup.caption: 1. Plant six seedlings in six pots. Label three Pinch and three Let Go.

setup.art: A child's fingers pinching a faded orange marigold flower off its stalk into a small bucket.
setup.caption: 2. Every visit, pinch off the faded flowers on the three Pinch plants.

setup.art: A Let Go marigold with a dry brown flower head full of seeds, and a Pinch marigold covered with fresh orange flowers.
setup.caption: 3. Let Go plants make seed heads. Pinch plants keep making flowers.

setup.art: A line graph with two lines, one for the Pinch group rising high and one for the Let Go group flat.
setup.caption: 4. At the end, draw a line graph of the flowers for each group.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pinch or Let Go. You guess before you plant.
flow.do: Show your child the seedlings. Explain that three plants will have their old flowers pinched off and three will not. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Marigolds flower for a long time. We will pinch the old flowers off three plants. The other three keep their flowers to make seeds. After eight weeks, which group will have more flowers? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pinch three plants. Leave three alone. Which group flowers more? Why?

ask.q: Why might pinching off old flowers make a plant flower longer?
good: The plant tries again to make seeds.
The plant has more energy for new flowers.
The plant does not waste food on seeds.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Gardeners call pinching off old flowers deadheading. Best months to start are October to January. In peak summer heat or a heavy monsoon, seedlings struggle. Nurseries often sell marigolds already in bud, which gives flowers sooner.

flow.context: In this step you plant the six seedlings and label them.
flow.do: 1. Fill six pots with soil. 2. Plant one seedling in each pot, at the same depth as the seedling was before. 3. Water well. 4. Label three P1, P2 and P3 and three L1, L2 and L3. 5. Put all six pots side by side in the sun.
flow.say: Plant all six the same way. Same soil, same sun, same water. Only the pinching will be different. Put the labels on the pots, not on the plants.
flow.kid: Plant six seedlings the same way. Label three Pinch and three Let Go. Put them in the sun.
flow.parent: Pick seedlings of the same size and health. Water every day or two, so the soil is damp but not soggy. Keep the pots where they get at least five hours of direct sun. Marigolds like heat.

check.q: Why do all six plants get the same soil, the same sun and the same water?
options: So only the pinching is different
So the pots look alike
So the plants grow tall
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the Let Go plants sat in the shade, we would not know whether the pinching or the shade made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you count and pinch each week for seven weeks.
flow.do: Every week for seven weeks: 1. Count the open flowers on each plant. 2. Write the number. 3. On the Pinch plants, pinch off every faded or dry flower. 4. Leave the Let Go plants alone. 5. Water the plants.
flow.say: Count the open flowers on each plant. Write down the numbers. Pinch off the faded flowers on the Pinch plants only. Leave the other three alone.
flow.kid: Count the open flowers on each plant. Pinch the old flowers on the Pinch plants only.
flow.parent: Count only the open, fresh flowers, not the buds or the dry ones. Expect no flowers in the first week or two, because the seedlings are small. If a plant dies, say so in your notes and carry on with the rest. Pinching means taking off the whole flower head just above the first leaf. Wash your hands afterwards. Who: one child can look after all six pots. With 2 to 4 children, one child looks after the Pinch pots and another the Let Go pots, and they swap and count each other's plants, so the counts are fair. Three plants in a group is a small sample: if there is no clear difference, say so.
flow.wait: Every week for 6 weeks, about 5 minutes

flow.context: In this step you add up the flowers, draw the graph and look at the seeds.
flow.do: 1. At week eight, count the open flowers on each plant for the last time. 2. Add up the flowers for each group, week by week. 3. Draw a line graph with a line for each group. 4. Collect the dry seed heads from the Let Go plants and open one.
flow.say: Add up the flowers for each group. Which group had more? Look at the dry seed heads. What is inside?
flow.kid: Add up the flowers. Draw the graph. Open a dry seed head.

ask.q: What do you notice about the two groups?
good: The Pinch group has more flowers.
The Let Go plants have dry seed heads.
They look about the same.

flow.parent: In most cases the Pinch plants flower for longer, and make more flowers, while the Let Go plants slow down once the seed heads are full. If your results are different, or the difference is small, say so. Three plants are a small sample, and plants differ. Dry seed heads from marigolds are packed with long thin black and tan seeds, and you can save them.

flow.context: In this step you say what the project showed, with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think about pinching and flowers? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: pinching off old flowers makes marigolds flower for longer. What I saw: the Pinch plants had more flowers than the Let Go plants in the last weeks. Why: a flower that has made seeds tells the plant that the job is nearly done, and the plant spends food on the seeds. When we pinch, the plant tries again with new flowers. A plant that is allowed to make seeds slows down.
flow.think: If a plant that is allowed to make seeds slows down, what does that tell you about why some plants die after seeding?

challenges.title: Ripe on Time: have a mango ready for a family dinner
challenges.problem: Your family is having a dinner in four days. You need one hard green mango to be soft and ripe on that day, no sooner and no later. Design the best way to ripen it, using only things from the kitchen.
challenges.safety: A grown-up cuts and checks the mangoes at the end. Wash the mangoes before eating. Do not give mango to anyone who is allergic to it, and mango sap can sting the skin. Do not eat any fruit that smells sour or looks rotten. Do not use carbide to ripen fruit. It is dangerous, and it is not allowed.
constraints: Use one hard green mango for each design. All the mangoes must be the same kind and size.
Use only ripe bananas or other ripe fruit, paper bags or boxes, cloth, newspaper, uncooked rice and a plate. No heater, stove, carbide or sealed plastic bag.
Every design must be opened for fresh air at least once a day.
On the dinner day, press each mango. The one closest to a soft, ripe mango, but not too mushy, is the winner.
materials: 3 or 4 hard green mangoes of the same kind and size, chosen with a little yellow tinge at the stalk if you can. Out of mango season, use green bananas from one hand instead.
2 or 3 very ripe bananas or an apple
paper bags, a cardboard box, a cloth and old newspaper
about 1 kilogram of uncooked rice in a big bowl or basket, for the burying design. Wash and use it normally afterwards.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about ripening. You use what you know about the ripening gas to plan how to ripen a mango in a set time.
general: A paper bag with one ripe banana, opened once a day.
A cardboard box with a loose cloth lid and a ripe banana, opened once a day.
A basket of rice with the mango buried halfway and a cloth over the top.
creative: Two ripe bananas in a bag with the mango, to make the gas stronger.
A layer of newspaper around the mango inside a box, so the warmth and gas stay close.
A ripe apple instead of a banana, since an apple also gives off a lot of ethylene.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own plan. Draw it, build it and press the mango each day. Did your mango get ripe on dinner day? What would you change?

setup.art: Four different set-ups on a table: a paper bag with a banana, a box with a cloth, a basket of rice and a mango alone.
setup.caption: 1. Build each design. Put one mango in each.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Ripe on Time challenge. You plan before you build.

ask.q: What do you know about how fruit ripen?
good: A ripe fruit makes a gas.
Warmth helps.
The fruit also needs fresh air.

flow.parent: Who: one child builds two or three designs and compares them. With 2 to 4 children, each child invents one design and owns one mango, and the whole group presses all the mangoes each day. Honest warning: a very hard, sour raw mango can need a week to soften, so four days may not be enough. A mango with a yellow tinge is more likely to be ripe in four days. If none is ready, that is a result. Say what you would change.

flow.context: In this step you build your designs and check them each day.
flow.do: 1. Build your designs. 2. Put a mango in each. 3. Label each. 4. Every day, open each design for a minute and press the mango. 5. Write down the softness from 1 to 5.
flow.say: Build your plan. Put the mango in. Each day open it up for fresh air. Press the mango. How soft is it?
flow.kid: Build your design. Open it every day. Press the mango.
flow.parent: Keep all the designs in the same warm room. Do not use plastic bags, which hold in water and can make fruit rot. Expect the open mango to be the slowest.

check.q: Why must every design be opened for fresh air once a day?
options: Fruit breathe, and in a sealed space they spoil instead of ripening
So the banana can see out
So the mango cools down
check.why: Ripening fruit use oxygen. In a sealed space, the oxygen runs low and the fruit spoils. A short airing each day keeps both the gas and the air.

flow.wait: Check each day for four days

flow.context: In this step you press the mangoes on the dinner day and pick the winner.
flow.do: On the dinner day: 1. Press each mango. 2. Rate the softness from 1 to 5. 3. Find the one closest to 4. 4. Cut the best mango open. 5. Write down what each design did.
flow.say: Dinner day! Press each mango. Which is soft but not mushy? Which design worked best? Why?
flow.kid: Press each mango. Which is softest but not mushy? Which design won?
flow.parent: A rating of 4 is soft, with a good smell and yellow colour. A rating of 5 is very soft and starting to spoil. If none of the mangoes is ripe, say so, and say what you would change. Cut open only the best mangoes and eat them if they smell sweet.
flow.think: If you had five days, would you change your plan? What would you do if you had only two?

challenges.title: Keep the Greens Green: store coriander for a week
challenges.problem: A bunch of coriander goes yellow and slimy in the fridge within days. Design the best way to keep four bunches fresh and green for seven days.
challenges.safety: Do not eat coriander that has turned slimy or smells bad. Wash your hands afterwards. Wash coriander well before you eat any.
constraints: Use bunches of coriander of the same kind, size and freshness.
Use only things from the kitchen: boxes, jars, bags, cloth, paper towels, water.
No freezer, and no store-bought chemicals.
On day 7, rate each bunch from 1 for fresh green to 5 for yellow or slimy, and count the yellow or slimy leaves out of 10 leaves taken at random.
materials: 4 fresh bunches of coriander, as alike as you can find
jars, a plastic box, paper towels, a cloth and a paper bag
a ripe banana, for the one test where it sits nearby
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about keeping leaves fresh. Leaves yellow when they age, when they are in the dark, and when ripe fruit are near. You use all that to design the best way to store coriander.
general: Stand the stems in a jar of water and cover the leaves loosely with a bag.
Wrap the bunch in a damp paper towel and put it in a box with a loose lid.
Keep the bunch away from ripe fruit such as bananas and mangoes.
creative: Wrap the bunch in a dry cloth, and put it in a jar of water, in the fridge.
Trim the stems fresh every two days, and take away any yellow leaves.
Put the bunch in the fridge in a box with a small hole, so the gas can leave.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to store coriander. Draw it, set it up and rate it on day 7. Which design kept the coriander greenest? Why do you think it worked?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep the Greens Green challenge. You plan before you build.
flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the usual designs and the creative ones. Ask your child to sketch two or three plans.
flow.say: Coriander goes yellow in days. What makes a leaf age? What helps a leaf stay fresh? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three ways to keep coriander green for a week.

ask.q: What do you know that makes leaves turn yellow?
good: Being in the dark.
Ripe fruit nearby.
Drying out.

flow.parent: Who: one child sets up four designs. With 2 to 4 children, each child invents one design and keeps a bunch, and all rate all bunches on day 7. Coriander costs a few rupees a bunch. Choose bunches that look as alike as you can.

flow.context: In this step you set up the four storage designs.
flow.do: 1. Divide the coriander into four bunches. 2. Set up four ways of storing it. 3. Label each. 4. Put each in its place. 5. Write down the date and the plan for each.
flow.say: Four bunches, four plans. Keep the things that are the same, the same. Only the storage is different. Label everything.
flow.kid: Set up four ways to store coriander. Label each one. Write down your plans.
flow.parent: Use the freshest bunches you can find. Wash the stems, but do not wash the leaves, because water on leaves makes them slimy. Keep the bunches that need the fridge in the same part of the fridge.

check.q: In one test, a bunch of coriander sits in a closed box next to a ripe banana. What do you expect?
options: The leaves will probably yellow sooner
The leaves will stay greener
Nothing will change
check.why: A ripe banana gives off ethylene, which speeds up the ageing of leaves. Leaves stored near ripe fruit often yellow sooner.

flow.wait: Leave for 7 days, checking on day 3

flow.context: In this step you rate the four bunches on day 7 and pick the best design.
flow.do: On day 7: 1. Take out each bunch. 2. Rate it from 1 to 5, and count the yellow or slimy leaves out of 10 leaves. 3. Look for yellow, slimy or dried leaves. 4. Find the best design. 5. Write why it worked.
flow.say: A week has gone by. Which bunch is greenest? Which is slimiest? Which design won? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Rate each bunch from 1 to 5. Which design won? Why?
flow.parent: Designs that work best tend to be cool, damp at the stems, loosely covered so leaves can breathe, and far from ripe fruit. A sealed bag often makes leaves slimy. Your results may differ. Write down what you see.
flow.think: Why might a shop keep its greens far from its fruit?
