quiz.p: Which of these best explains why a ripe banana in a bag makes a raw mango ripen sooner?
opts: The banana gives off a gas that the mango can sense
The banana's sugar flows into the mango
The banana's skin sticks to the mango
quiz.why: The banana makes ethylene, which drifts through the air in the bag. Raw fruit have receptors that sense it, and they start to ripen too. Picking 'sugar flows' is a natural guess, but the banana and mango never touch.

quiz.p: As a mango ripens and tastes sweeter, what happens to the starch stored in the fruit?
quiz.why: Ripening turns stored starch into sugar. Picking 'stays the same' would leave the fruit hard and bland. Picking 'seeds' mixes up the food in a fruit with the new plants inside.

quiz.p: Which of these is the best way to ripen a hard green mango at home?
opts: A paper bag with a ripe banana, opened each day for fresh air
A sealed plastic bag in the fridge
A closed tin with a lid taped shut
quiz.why: Ripening needs warmth, a little ethylene and fresh air. A paper bag keeps the gas close and lets air in when opened. The fridge slows ripening, and a sealed tin runs short of air.

quiz.p: A carrot plant stores food in the root in the first year. What does the plant do with the food in the second year?
opts: Uses it to grow a flower stalk and make seeds
Gives it away to the soil
Stores it for a third year
quiz.why: A carrot is a biennial. The plant saves up food in year one, and spends it in year two on flowers and seeds. Then the plant dies. We usually eat the carrot before the plant flowers.

quiz.p: How does a fern make new ferns?
opts: With tiny spores that grow into a heart-shaped plant
With flowers and seeds, like a rose
quiz.why: A fern makes dust-like spores under the fronds. A spore grows on damp soil into a tiny heart-shaped plant, which makes eggs and sperm. The fertilised egg grows into a fern. Picking 'flowers and seeds' is the old mistaken idea about ferns.

quiz.p: A farmer takes a money plant cutting and roots it in water. How is the new plant related to the old plant?
opts: It is an exact copy, a clone of the old plant
It is a different kind of plant
It is the old plant's child, a little different
It is half the old plant and half a new plant
quiz.why: A cutting is a piece of the parent, so it has exactly the same instructions. A plant from a seed gets instructions from two parents, so the new plant is a little different. Picking 'a little different' describes a seedling.

quiz.p: Which of these plants is most likely to need a spell of winter cold before it flowers?
quiz.why: Apple trees come from cool places and need winter chill to flower well. Tomato, moong and sunflower flower without a cold spell. Picking 'tomato' mixes up fruit that grow in warmth with plants that need cold.

quiz.p: A tree has a very narrow ring among wide ones. What is the best explanation?
opts: That year was hard for the tree, such as a year of little rain
The tree was cut that year
The tree was planted that year
quiz.why: A tree grows less in a hard year, so the ring is narrow. A wide ring marks a good year. Picking 'planted that year' would put the narrow ring at the centre, in the first year, not among wide ones.

quiz.p: A palak leaf is kept in a dark cupboard for a week. What do you expect?
opts: The leaf goes yellow, because the plant cannot make food from it and begins to take it apart
The leaf stays exactly the same
quiz.why: Without light, a leaf cannot make food. The ageing programme starts, the chlorophyll is broken down, and the leaf turns yellow. Picking 'darker green' is the opposite of what happens.

quiz.p: Which of these plants flowers just once after waiting for many years, and then dies?
quiz.why: A talipot palm waits for more than 30 years, flowers once and dies. Mango, banyan and neem flower in many seasons. Picking 'banyan' mixes up a plant that lives long with a plant that flowers once.

quiz.p: The chart shows how soft three mangoes were after four days. How many softness points more did the mango in the bag with a ripe banana score than the mango left in the open?
quiz.why: The mango with the banana scored 4 and the mango in the open scored 2. 4 take away 2 is 2. Picking 4 means reading only the first bar, not the difference.
quiz.context: In the ripening bag test, three hard green mangoes are put in three places and rated for softness from 1 to 5. These numbers are made up.

chart.title: Made-up example: softness of the mangoes on day 4 (1 is hard, 5 is very soft)

quiz.p: Why do mango farmers graft a twig of their best tree onto young plants, instead of planting stones?
opts: The twig grows into a branch that bears the same fruit as the best tree
quiz.why: A graft is a piece of the best tree, so it gives the same fruit. Stones are seeds, and each seedling is a little different. Picking 'more variety' is the opposite, because a graft is a copy.

applications: Fruit traders ripen mangoes, bananas and papayas in warm rooms with small, controlled amounts of ethylene, so that the fruit is ripe on the day it is sold.
Cold stores slow the ripening of apples and other fruit for months, and remove ethylene from the air to keep the fruit from ripening too soon.
Bananas are picked green and shipped across the country, then ripened near the market, so that they arrive firm and undamaged.
Flower growers and florists cover chrysanthemums with dark cloth, or add lamps at night, to make the flowers open for a festival.
Gardeners pinch off old flowers from marigolds and zinnias, so that the plants keep flowering for longer.
Plant breeders choose rice and wheat varieties for their day-length sensitivity and cold needs, so that the crop flowers at the right time in each region.
Farmers graft mango and guava trees to get the same fruit as their best tree, sooner than from a stone.
Tissue culture labs grow banana plants from tiny pieces of tissue, to supply clean, disease-free plants to farmers.
Scientists read the rings of teak and other trees to work out the monsoon rains of past centuries.
Archaeologists and furniture historians date old wooden beams by matching their ring patterns to trees of known age.
Kitchens that store leafy greens away from ripe fruit, and put a ripe banana next to a hard avocado, use ethylene without knowing its name.
Plant breeders are trying to develop perennial rice and wheat that regrow every year without replanting.

open_questions.q: What switches on the burst of ethylene when a fruit begins to ripen?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the genes and signals involved. Exactly what tips a fruit from waiting to ripening, and how the signals are timed, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Do damaged plants warn their neighbours on purpose, or do the neighbours only overhear?
open_questions.why_open: Many experiments show that plants respond to the scent of damaged neighbours. Whether the signal evolved as a warning, or the neighbours evolved to listen in, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How can a plant remember a winter for weeks, and how can a bamboo count decades?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found the chemical marks on genes that keep the memory of a winter for weeks. Nobody has found a clock that could count a bamboo's 48 years.

open_questions.q: Do trees grow old as animals do?
open_questions.why_open: Some trees show very little decline for centuries, and others decline slowly. It is hard to follow one tree for thousands of years, so the question is still open.

open_questions.q: Can we breed perennial grains, like perennial rice and wheat, that give as much grain as the annual crops?
open_questions.why_open: Perennial grains would save ploughing and sowing each year. Plant breeders are trying, but so far the harvests are smaller than those of annual crops.

open_questions.q: Why does an annual plant die after setting seed, when they could go on living?
open_questions.why_open: Two main ideas, a food drain and a chemical signal from the seeds, both have support. Scientists do not agree on which matters most, and it may differ from plant to plant.

maths.problem: A mango in a bag with a ripe banana is ripe after 3 days. A mango in the open takes 6 days. How many days sooner is the first mango? How many times as fast is it?
maths.answer: 3 days sooner. It ripens 2 times as fast.
maths.explain: 6 take away 3 is 3 days sooner. 6 divided by 3 is 2. So the mango with the banana ripened in half the time, which is twice as fast.
maths.context: In the ripening bag test, you compare how long the mangoes in different places take to ripen.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two times with a ratio tells you how much faster one way is, not just which is faster.

maths.problem: A teak log has 36 rings, and its outermost ring formed in 2019. In which year did the tree sprout?
maths.explain: If the 36th ring is from 2019, the first ring is 35 years earlier. 2019 take away 35 is 1984. A check: from 1984 to 2019, counting both years, is 36 years.
maths.context: Counting tree rings tells you how many years a tree lived, if the tree makes one ring a year.
maths.why_maths: Counting rings and counting back along the calendar turns a pattern in wood into a date.

maths.problem: On the lifespan tape, one millimetre stands for one year. A moong plant lives about 3 months. How many moong lifetimes fit into one millimetre? How long is the tape for the Sri Maha Bodhi tree, which is about 2,300 years old, in metres?
maths.answer: 4 moong lifetimes fit in a millimetre. The tape for the tree is 2.3 metres long.
maths.explain: 3 months is a quarter of a year, so 4 moong lifetimes make 1 year, which is 1 millimetre. 2,300 millimetres is 2 metres and 300 millimetres, which is 2.3 metres.
maths.context: In the Lifespan Tape activity, you draw a strip in which 1 millimetre stands for 1 year.
maths.why_maths: A scale lets you put the life of a moong plant and of an old tree on the same strip and compare them.

maths.problem: In the Pinch or Let Go project, the Pinch plants had 3, 8, 14, 20, 22 and 25 flowers at the six weekly counts, added over all three plants. The Let Go plants had 3, 6, 9, 8, 5 and 3. Which group had more flowers in total, and by how many?
maths.answer: The Pinch group had 92 flowers and the Let Go group 34. The Pinch group had 58 more.
maths.explain: 3 + 8 + 14 + 20 + 22 + 25 is 92. 3 + 6 + 9 + 8 + 5 + 3 is 34. 92 take away 34 is 58. The numbers are made up, but real pinched marigolds often flower for longer.
maths.context: In the project, you count the open flowers every week on plants whose old flowers are pinched off and plants whose flowers are left alone.
maths.why_maths: Adding the weekly counts for each group lets you compare two lines of numbers with a single total.

maths.problem: Mizoram bamboo flowered around 2006. The bamboo flowers about every 48 years. About what year will it flower next? A child who is 10 years old in 2026 will be how old then?
maths.explain: 2006 + 48 = 2054. A child who is 10 in 2026 was born in 2016. 2054 take away 2016 is 38. So the child will be about 38.
maths.context: Some bamboos flower all together once in about 48 years and then die.
maths.why_maths: Adding the period to the last flowering predicts the next one, and the difference between years gives an age.

maths.problem: A farm has 5 kinds of banana in equal numbers. A disease harms only one kind. What fraction of the plants is harmed? What fraction would be harmed if the farm had only one kind?
maths.answer: One fifth. If there were only one kind, all of the plants, which is 5 out of 5.
maths.explain: With 5 kinds in equal numbers, each kind is 1 out of 5 of the plants. The disease harms 1 of the 5 kinds, so 1 fifth of the plants. With one kind, the disease can harm every plant, which is 5 out of 5, or the whole farm.
maths.context: Bananas grown from suckers are clones, so every plant of one kind has the same weakness to a disease.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how variety limits the damage a disease can do.

maths.problem: Suppose, as a made-up rule, that one ripe banana can ripen about 4 raw mangoes in a loosely closed box. How many ripe bananas would you need for 40 mangoes?
maths.explain: Each banana covers 4 mangoes. 40 divided by 4 is 10. So 10 ripe bananas would be needed, if the made-up rule held.
maths.context: In a ripening box, a ripe banana gives off the gas that tells raw mangoes to ripen.
maths.why_maths: A rule such as one banana for four mangoes can be turned into a plan for any number of mangoes by division.

maths.problem: Marigold seedlings cost 5 rupees each. A pot costs 25 rupees. How much do 6 seedlings and 6 pots cost together?
maths.explain: 6 seedlings at 5 rupees is 30 rupees. 6 pots at 25 rupees is 150 rupees. 30 + 150 is 180 rupees.
maths.context: In the Pinch or Let Go project, you buy six seedlings and six pots.
maths.why_maths: Working out the cost shows what a plan needs before you start it.

roots.context: We tested how a ripe banana ripens a raw mango without touching. Now we ask what this message through the air tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the bag, a ripe banana and a raw mango never touched, yet the mango ripened sooner. A gas called ethylene passed between them through the air. So a ripe fruit sends a message, and a raw fruit nearby hears it and answers.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a fruit as a finished thing that sits alone and changes only with time. But a fruit senses, makes a gas, and answers the gas of the fruit next to them. Ripening is something fruit do together.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bag test, a mango sharing a bag with a ripe banana softened and yellowed days before a mango in a bag alone. A mango in the open was slowest. If your own result differed, write down what happened.

three.who_am_i: A yawn can spread across a room, and a smell of rain can change your mood, without anyone touching you. You change people near you through the air, and they change you.
three.what_is_life: A ripe fruit is alive and awake. They sense, make a gas, and call to their neighbours. Plants speak to each other with gases, as people speak with voices.
three.what_is_this_world: A bag of fruit, an orchard and a forest each carry news from plant to plant through the air. Nothing alive is truly alone.

roots.thread: One gas, made by one ripe fruit, spreads through a whole bunch of fruit, and the whole bunch ripens together. Each fruit is separate, yet the bunch acts like one body. The gas is a tiny molecule of just six atoms, and it joins them. So separateness and togetherness are both true here: there are many fruit, and there is one ripening.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, on interbeing, in The Heart of Understanding
teachings.teaching: If you are a poet, you will see clearly that there is a cloud floating in this sheet of paper. Without a cloud there is no rain, without rain the trees cannot grow, and without trees we cannot make paper.
teachings.link: A mango that ripens because of a banana has a banana in it, in a way. What a fruit becomes depends on the fruit around them.

teachings.source: Purananuru 192, a Tamil poem by Kaniyan Pungundranar from the Sangam age
teachings.teaching: Every town is our town. Everyone is our kin.
teachings.link: Fruit in one bag act like kin. What one fruit does for itself spreads to all the rest.

teachings.teaching: All things grow and flower, and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is stillness.
teachings.link: A plant flowers, makes seeds, yellows and falls. What was in the leaves goes into the seeds and back to the soil. The ending carries on into the next beginning.

science.text: Ripe fruit give off ethylene, a gas that speeds the ripening of fruit nearby. Plants have receptors that catch the gas.
Whether plants send each other warnings through scent molecules, and whether the neighbours are listening on purpose, is still argued about.

other_view.view: The banana does not speak to the mango. A gas is released as part of the banana's own ripening, and the mango reacts to the chemical, as iron reacts to damp. Calling this a message or a conversation is a way of talking that adds an idea the chemistry does not need.

practice.title: Smell the message
practice.say: Hold a ripe banana in one hand and a raw mango in the other. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Notice the sweet smell of the banana. That smell is the fruit sending a message into the air. Breathe in slowly three times. What do you think the raw mango is doing right now?
practice.kid: Hold a ripe banana. Close your eyes. Breathe in the smell, slowly, three times. The fruit is sending a message through the air.

ask: When a banana and a mango share a bag, are there two fruit, or one ripening?
If a raw mango hears a banana, is the mango listening, or just reacting?
What else in your day travels between you and others without a touch?

how_we_found_out.story: For years, citrus growers in the United States noticed that lemons turned yellow sooner in sheds heated with kerosene stoves. Everyone thought that the warmth of the stove did the work. In the 1920s, an American plant scientist, F. E. Denny, tested this. Other scientists had already found that a gas in the shed air, not the warmth, seemed to do the work. Denny reported that the active gas in the stove fumes was ethylene, and that even a tiny amount turned green lemons yellow. So the warmth was not the cause. A gas in the smoke was. In 1934, an English plant scientist, Richard Gane, showed that ripening fruit make ethylene themselves. A fruit does not need a stove at all. A ripe fruit makes the gas, and the gas ripens the fruit nearby.
how_we_found_out.who: F. E. Denny, an American plant scientist, and Richard Gane, an English plant scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Growers believed that the heat of the stoves coloured the lemons. Tests that kept the temperature the same and changed only the gas showed that the gas alone made the difference.
